sources.news_title: Nine people dead in Learjet crash in south Florida
sources.text:
Florida - A Learjet crashed on Sunday afternoon in a residential area in Palm Beach County, Florida, killing all nine people on board, United States transportation officials said.
The private jet had taken off from Austin-Bergstrom International Airport in Texas and was headed to North Eleuthera Airport in the Bahamas, the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) said in a statement. Videos on social media showed the jet slamming into the ground next to a road and exploding. “It was a big-time tragedy that happened,” Florida Governor Ron DeSantis said at a press conference near the crash site in Lake Worth Beach. “When you see that video, it’s a jarring thing. It was like a missile coming down, and a massive explosion, debris going everywhere.” The National Transportation Safety Board said it had launched an investigation into the crash, which Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy called a “horrific tragedy.”
FAA records list the Bombardier-made Learjet 60’s owner as a Delaware corporation. Canada-based Bombardier said it would fully support the investigation and cooperate as needed. The crash left a “massive crater” by the road near the entrance to a mobile home park, Palm Beach County Commissioner Joel Flores said at the news conference. About 600 people were being evacuated from the area and relocated to two shelters in the county, Flores said.
Heavy rainfall and thunderstorms were occurring in the area at the time, forecaster AccuWeather said in a statement. An audio recording from a Miami air traffic control centre posted on LiveATC, a site that broadcasts air traffic control communications, captured the plane’s final moments before the crash in unusual detail. At first, someone in the plane’s cockpit reported to an air traffic controller that they were “managing the ice” but faced “moderate” turbulence and were seeking “better rides”. Less than a minute later, the person said “Mayday, mayday,” reporting that the plane was suddenly descending at a rate of 10,000 feet per minute.
Seconds later, the person said they were declaring an emergency, with the rate of descent accelerating to 20,000 feet per minute. Less than 20 seconds later, the person said: “We’re going to crash into the ground” before saying that the descent rate had reached 22,000 feet per minute as the plane started banking.
About 35 seconds after the initial mayday announcement, the last thing heard from the cockpit was a rapidly spoken “We’re out of time.”
Flight tracking website Flightradar24 said data showed the vertical descent rate at one point exceeded 32,000 feet per minute.

Palm Beach plane crash footage isn’t AI-generated, despite social media claims
sources.text: By — Maria Briceño, PolitiFact Maria Briceño, PolitiFact Leave your feedback Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/nation/palm-beach-plane-crash-footage-isnt-ai-generated-despite-social-media-claims Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Palm Beach plane crash footage isn't AI-generated, despite social media claims Nation Nov 2, 2026 5:24 PM EST This article originally appeared on PolitiFact. Footage from Palm Beach County, Florida, shows a plane nosediving into the ground at full speed, cratering the pavement, and dissolving into fire and smoke. It looks unreal. So unreal that some social media users say it's fake. Stand with free and independent journalism. Join Press Pass from PBS News "The Video You're All Seeing From The 'Plane' Crash Was 100% Ai Generated SOMEONE IS LYING TO US !!!!!! That Was Not An Airplane," read a Nov. 1 X post sharing video of what looks like an AI detection video analysis. "Notice How The Ai Detector Only Detects Ai Generated Content From The 'Plane.'" Other X posts also questioned the footage's veracity. But the crash happened and the video has been corroborated by legitimate news outlets. A business jet, a Learjet 60, was headed to the Bahamas from Austin, Texas, when it crashed into a neighborhood near Cresthaven, Florida, at approximately 12:51 p.m. ET, on Nov. 1. Everyone on board died, U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said Nov. 1. The authorities have not said what caused the crash, but Tom Chapman, a member of the National Transportation Safety Board, said Nov. 2 that the aircraft experienced turbulence and encountered ice. The incident is under investigation, he said at a press conference that day. Timothy Monville, who's leading the investigation into the crash for the safety board, said the federal agency has "just begun" documenting the incident. "We have a lot of work to do on scene," he said. "This will be a several-day process, and the biggest obstacle that we're going to have is recovering the major wreckage from the impacted crater on the roadway." The crash footage has been shared by The Associated Press, CNN, CBS News and BBC. We also found its original source, Aki Kuusisto, a digital creator from West Palm Beach, who first shared the clip on Facebook. "This was not quite what I had in mind when I installed the dash cam," Kuusisto said in the post's comments. The X posts show screen recordings of the clip being submitted to Hive Moderation, an AI-detection tool. The recordings show the tool's analysis reporting that it detected AI-generated content in the clip. Hive Moderation is an imperfect tool and PolitiFact has used it before. However, when we introduced Kuusisto's footage to the tool, it didn't flag it as AI-generated or manipulated. Flames rise following an aircraft incident in Palm Beach County, Florida, on Nov. 1, 2026, in this still image obtained from video. Photo by Eduin Cruz via Reuters Darren Linvill, co-director of the Media Forensics Hub at Clemson University, told PolitiFact people are right to be skeptical of viral videos as AI improves. But some people have grown so distrustful of AI they're disbelieving the truth, a phenomenon known as the "liar's dividend." "This is when people are so accustomed to being lied to, they don't know the truth when it is presented to them," Linvill said. "That is what is occurring with the video of the Palm Beach crash." It's not surprising the crash was captured on camera considering how abundant personal recording devices are today. But Linvill added that people should get their news from reliable sources. One of the X accounts that questioned the veracity of the plane crash footage, for example, has been amplified by bot accounts that promote narratives by Russian Storm-1516, a campaign that uses Russian and non-Russian influencers to promote false claims in the U.S. and other countries. Our ruling An X post said footage of Nov. 1 plane crash in Palm Beach County, Florida, "was 100%" generated with artificial intelligence News outlets have shared the dash cam footage confirming the video's veracity. An AI expert told PolitiFact that although the video is dramatic and frightening, it is authentic. We rate this claim Pants on Fire! A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. Support trusted journalism and civil dialogue. Donate now By — Maria Briceño, PolitiFact Maria Briceño, PolitiFact

sources.news_title: Fiery Jet Crash In Florida Kills 9 After Falling 20,000 Feet Per Minute Before Impact
sources.text:
Fiery Jet Crash In Florida Kills 9 After Falling 20,000 Feet Per Minute Before Impact
Just seconds after the co-pilot of flight N722BD sent its Mayday final transmission on Sunday afternoon, the private Learjet 60 crashed in a fiery explosion, killing all 9 people on board and raining debris across a South Florida community. As of Monday, authorities are still in the early stages of the investigation, which could take several days to collect wreckage from the fallen aircraft, according to AP News.
According to the National Transportation Safety Board, the business jet took off from Austin, Texas, and was heading towards the Bahamas when it hit the ground in the Palm Beach County neighborhood of Green Acres, near West Palm Beach. Just minutes before the crash, the co-pilot, 20-year-old Nathalia Filgueiras, reported encountering weather causing icing and "moderate turbulence." They asked to ascend to 37,000 feet, which was approved by Air Traffic Control. The plane then began descending quickly, with the co-pilot informing controllers, "We're descending 8,000 — Mayday, Mayday — we're descending 10,000 feet per minute.
One pilot has been identified as of this writing. Filgueiras was a Boca Raton resident who achieved her dream of a pilot's license while still in high school and had 1,300 hours of flying time under her belt. She was the one who made the final emergency calls as the jet went down. Another pilot was aboard the flight as well. It is unclear at this time who was at the controls of the jet when the crash occurred. All nine fatalities were passengers onboard the plane.
During a news conference Monday the NTSB officials said the crash created a debris field approximately a half mile by four-tenths of a mile, but it may be larger as there is evidence that shows the plane was likely breaking up prior to impact. They've asked members of the community who find debris to not move it and contact NTSB or local authorities to handle it. Officials also said that weather conditions are being considered as a major factor in the events that unfolded Sunday afternoon. More updates are expected to come in the following days.
Everything was engulfed in flames
In the plane's final transmissions, the plane was flying at an altitude of nearly 9,000 feet. The plane then nosedived, falling at 32,000 feet per minute according to CBS News, however, the NTSB said those numbers have not yet been determined or confirmed. Dashcam footage shared with multiple news outlets caught the moment of impact from the back of a moving vehicle on a divided motorway. Another dashcam video obtained by KCEN 6 News, showed the plane falling out of the sky some distance ahead of the vehicle before impact.
Witnesses to the crash told CBS News it sounded like a bomb went off when the jet hit the ground. Stephanie Platts, a resident at a neighboring mobile home community park, told The New York Times she was on her patio with her family when the plane hit, which sounded like a car crash. Her home caught fire from some of the raining debris.
"Everything was engulfed in flames," she said.
Palm Beach County authorities were called to the scene where it was eventually confirmed that all nine passengers on board the business jet had died. Only one individual may have sustained injuries from the crash, who was adjacent to the scene, but officials have yet to confirm that injury.
This crash comes just months after an Amazon Air cargo plane killed five people after landing late on a Miami runway. Weeks later, a small yellow airplane narrowly missed hitting a postal van while making an emergency landing on an Illinois highway, leaving no crashes or injuries behind.

In the final moments before a private jet crashed in Florida, killing all nine people aboard, someone reportedly turned to one of Christianity’s most familiar prayers.
According to the New York Post, a male voice could apparently be heard reciting part of the Lord’s Prayer as the aircraft rapidly descended toward the ground on Sunday, Nov. 1.
“Who art in heaven, hallowed be the name,” the voice reportedly said.
The chilling recording offers a glimpse into the desperate final moments aboard the doomed flight.
The Learjet 60 was traveling from Austin, Texas, to the Bahamas when the crew encountered dangerous conditions. According to Reuters, the pilots reported ice and moderate turbulence before the aircraft suddenly began plummeting toward the ground.
As the situation deteriorated, 20-year-old co-pilot Nathalia Filgueiras reportedly described the terrifying descent.

As the aircraft continued its rapid descent, another devastating statement was heard by Filgueiras: “We’re out of time.”
The aircraft crashed near Cresthaven in Palm Beach County around 12:50 p.m., leaving behind a massive crater and flames near residential homes.

sources.news_title: Lenny Kravitz’s Rep Debunks Rumor He Was Involved in Fatal Florida Learjet Crash
sources.text: Lenny Kravitz’s Rep Debunks Rumor He Was Involved in Fatal Florida Learjet Crash A private jet crashed in Florida on Sunday, Nov. 1, killing all nine people on board By Rachel DeSantis Rachel DeSantis Rachel DeSantis is a senior writer on the music team at PEOPLE. She has been working at PEOPLE since 2019, and her work has previously appeared in Entertainment Weekly and the New York Daily News. People Editorial Guidelines Updated on November 2, 2026 02:00PM EST Leave a Comment Add Us On Lenny Kravitz at the MTV Video Music Awards in New York in September 2024. Credit : Angela Weiss/AFP/Getty NEED TO KNOW Lenny Kravitz’s representative confirmed that he was not on board a plane that crashed in Florida, despite viral rumors The jet was traveling from Austin, Texas, to the Bahamas when it crashed, killing nine people Co-pilot Nathalia Filgueiras, 20, was the first confirmed victim Lenny Kravitz was not on board the Learjet 60 business jet that crashed in Florida this weekend, despite viral internet rumors that suggested he was. Reports that the musician, 62, was involved in the fatal crash on Sunday, Nov. 1 are “untrue and incorrect,” a rep for the star confirms to PEOPLE. Kravitz was rumored to be on board the flight after screenshots that were widely disseminated on social media featured a young female pilot posting that she was “honored” to be flying the star from Austin, Texas, to the Bahamas the next day. It remains unclear whether the screenshots were legitimate, though the pilot later wrote on TikTok that she was not involved in the crash, which killed all nine people on board. The doomed flight took off from Austin-Bergstrom International Airport in Texas and was headed to North Eleuthera Airport in the Bahamas, according to the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA). Closed roads after a jet crash in Greenacres, Fla. on Nov. 1, 2026. Saul Martinez/Getty Related Stories Co-Pilot, 20, Identified in Private Plane Crash That Left 9 Dead After Frantic Mayday Call Private Plane Crashes in Florida Neighborhood, Killing All 9 People on Board Minutes before it went down, the jet reported an accumulation of ice and said it was jolting as much as 700 feet due to turbulence, according to air traffic control radio. Video footage of the incident showed the plane hitting the ground in a fiery crash, leaving a large crater in the ground and causing a number of fires around the site. The co-pilot was identified as 20-year-old Nathalia Filgueiras of Boca Raton, Fla., according to The New York Times. The other victims have not been identified. Filgueiras earned her pilot’s license at 17, and had logged more than 1,300 hours of flight time prior to the crash, per the Times. “She loved the freedom,” her mother Camila Corteleti told the outlet. “It was completely different seeing the world from the top.” VIPs Get More The PEOPLE stories you love, with first access and special features reserved for subscribers. Subscribe Now Additional victims included Adam Robinson and his wife Helen Sharp, their children Emma and Charlie, Rachael Reed, Charmi Fehr and Anita Maria Cetina. “With broken hearts, our families share that Adam Robinson and Helen Sharp, their children Emma and Charlie, Rachael Reed and Charmi Fehr, and Anita Maria Cetina were among those lost aboard the flight that went down near Greenacres, Florida, on November 1,” their families said in a joint statement. “Adam and Helen were devoted parents, and Emma, 4, and Charlie, 2, were the light of their lives. Helen and Adam were the love affair that will last forever. Their warmth, generosity and gift for making people feel welcome touched so many lives. Their loss will be felt deeply by all those who loved them and who they loved in return.” The statement continued, “Charmi and Rachel were full of joy and adventure. They loved their people fiercely, fully and without hesitation. From the moment they met, they were all in on each other and the life they were building. They are deeply loved, and we will miss them endlessly. Anita Maria cared for Emma and Charlie with tenderness and devotion, and she was truly part of the family. She showed us a legacy of unconditional love and devotion. We are deeply grateful to the first responders, investigators, and the Palm Beach County community for their care, and to everyone who has reached out with love. Our hearts are also with the families of the pilots, who are grieving alongside us. We ask for privacy as we grieve. Details about memorial services will be shared once arrangements are made.” The jet crashed in a residential area near Cresthaven, Fla. around 12:50 p.m. local time. Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis said that due to the debris and damage caused by the crash to the surrounding infrastructure, 600 residents were being assisted with temporary shelter and other essential needs. The crash is under investigation by the National Transportation Safety Board. Leave a Comment Read More: Entertainment Music Rock Music

sources.news_title: Victims of Florida plane crash include a 20-year-old who got her pilot's license as a teen
sources.text:
Victims of Florida plane crash include a 20-year-old copilot and tech entrepreneur and his family
Posted November 2, 2026 12:45 pm.
Last Updated November 2, 2026 6:12 pm.
A 20-year-old woman who had been a licensed pilot since she was a teenager and a technology entrepreneur and his family were among nine people killed when a small jet crashed and exploded in South Florida, family members said.
Nathalia Gadelha Filgueiras was the copilot flying a Learjet from Austin, Texas, to the Bahamas, on Sunday when it crashed and exploded near West Palm Beach, her mother Camila Corteleti told the New York Post and New York Times.
Filgueiras earned her license in 2023 when she was a 17-year-old senior at West Boca Raton Community High School, according to local news reports at the time.
The crash also killed Adam Robinson, his wife, Helen Sharp, and their children, 4-year-old Emma and 2-year-old Charlie, according to a statement from the families of the seven passengers. Anita Maria Cetina, who helped care for the children, also died.
Two more victims were identified as Rachael Reed and Charmi Fehr. The identity of the other pilot was not immediately disclosed.
Robinson built tech companies
“Our hearts are also with the families of the pilots, who are grieving alongside us,” the families of the seven said.
Robinson recently told the ProfitLed podcast that he and his family lived in Aspen, Colorado. He was a co-founder of Robly, an email marketing platform, and founder of Retention.com, which uses technology to connect e-commerce website visitors to their email addresses.
“I feel like I’m living the dream,” Robinson, 45, said.
“I love the fact that I get to see my kids in the morning and the evening, and I don’t have to travel for work that much, and I get to live in this place that’s always been my dream,” he said. “And my wife is super happy because she can be a full-time artist.”
Robinson was known in Austin, Texas, where Retention.com was based. It’s the second time this year that Austin has lost a tech entrepreneur in a plane crash, following the June death of Joshua Baer, who led a venture capital firm that supported tech startups.
“Adam was part of the entrepreneurial fabric of Austin,” said Thom Singer, CEO of the Austin Technology Council, which promotes the local industry.
Pilot joked about her youth and skills
Filgueiras’ pilot’s license showed she had the rating to fly the jet but not to be in command of the flight.
The Palm Beach County School District paid for her license as part of the high school’s specialized aviation academy, in which students practice flying on simulators and drones.
“Some people think that it’s weird that I can fly planes, but I can’t drive a car,” Filgueiras told WPEC-TV in 2023. “I think it’s funny.”
Ed White, The Associated Press

sources.news_title: Business jet plunges near Trump’s Florida residence: What caused the crash?
sources.text:
A business jet crashed in a Florida residential neighbourhood, 14 kilometres from Donald Trump's estate, on the eve of the elections. Experts cite sudden icing as the cause. But is that really what happened?
Official information from the investigation into the Learjet 60 crash in Florida indicates that it was a tragic aviation accident caused by difficult weather conditions, with no connection to any deliberate action or an "attack" on Donald Trump.
Suspicion arose because Mar-a-Lago, Trump's main headquarters, residence and personal "fortress" in Florida, is located just 14 kilometres from the crash site. The second factor was that the accident occurred one day before the congressional elections.
The aircraft was operating a routine commercial flight from Austin, Texas, to the Bahamas. Palm Beach lay along its route, and the crash occurred in a residential suburb as the jet approached an area of challenging weather conditions.
According to preliminary expert assessments, the pilots entered a thunderstorm cloud that was developing too rapidly, causing a sudden and explosive increase in cloud formation. A powerful updraft developed, the temperature dropped to -47°C, and supercooled moisture rapidly froze onto the wings and tail. Attempting to deal with the icing, the crew requested an emergency climb and received clearance. However, the aircraft entered a steep dive, reaching a speed of 365 km/h near the ground.
On the Learjet 60, the leading edges of the wings and tail are heated with hot air drawn from the engines using a system known as anti-ice. The aircraft's onboard systems can cope with ordinary icing. However, judging by the recorded radio communications, the crew encountered an unusually rapid and intense accumulation of ice.
By the time the pilot told air traffic control, "We have light, clear ice that is manageable", the situation was already critical. Within minutes, the heating system simply could not melt the rapidly forming layer of ice. This led to an aerodynamic deadlock and a sudden loss of control, sending the aircraft into a steep dive.
Some technical analyses suggest that the aircraft remained an intact flying object until the very last moment, as the wing controls (ailerons) were still functioning, while longitudinal control through the tail had failed completely.
Because footage from vehicle dashcams shows the aircraft falling almost vertically at high speed, some social media commentators have written that "this looks more like a falling missile than an aircraft". Florida Governor Ron DeSantis fuelled this interpretation at a press conference, casually remarking that the fall had visually "looked like a missile coming down". Trump supporters began widely circulating rumours that the Learjet 60 might have been shot down by air defence systems deployed by the military around Mar-a-Lago, either by mistake or because it was a suicide aircraft.
Trump is campaigning for re-election and makes several flights a day aboard his personal Boeing 757, known as Trump Force One. The destruction of a business jet of a similar class in his "home territory" is being interpreted as a warning that the skies are no longer a safe place for him and his inner circle, and that any technical or weather-related anomaly could be staged. According to this line of reasoning, the incident is intended to force Trump and his team to divert their attention to domestic security, sow panic within campaign headquarters and disrupt the politician's normal routine.
Those who reject this conspiracy theory argue that terrorists deliberately direct an aircraft towards a target while maintaining control of the flight. By contrast, they say, the Learjet 60's vertical descent in an aerodynamic stall could not physically have been deliberately replicated using the controls. It was the result of a complete breakdown of airflow over an ice-covered wing. The aircraft fell like a stone rather than flying towards Trump's residence.
As for the possibility that the jet was hit by an anti-aircraft missile, critics argue that air defence systems do not shoot down objects "blindly" simply because their flight path looks suspicious. The Learjet 60 was neither an unidentified object nor a target that had suddenly appeared. It was following a clearly authorised civilian route, its transponder was operating continuously, and the pilots remained in constant contact with Miami air traffic controllers until the final seconds, transmitting a distress signal over the radio.
Whatever the truth, American society is divided into two irreconcilable camps, which have yet to show what they are capable of when it comes to destroying one another.

The flight had departed Austin-Bergstrom International Airport in Texas and was bound for North Eleuthera Airport in the Bahamas when it crashed in Palm Beach County.
U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy confirmed Sunday evening that all nine people aboard the aircraft were killed.
“Today’s plane crash in Palm Beach County, Florida is a horrific tragedy,” Duffy said in a public statement. “Here’s what we know: At 12:50 PM ET, a Learjet 60 crashed in a neighborhood near Cresthaven, FL. Describing the scene as “jarring,” DeSantis commended Palm Beach County Sheriff’s deputies and local fire rescue crews for moving rapidly to suppress flames and stabilize an area strewn with burning debris.
“Obviously, this was a cataclysmic plane crash. It looked like a missile going down. As of now, we don’t have any reports of anyone who was on the ground apart from the people in the plane who were killed or injured as a result of debris. But the debris was significant and went over a pretty significant distance.”
DeSantis confirmed state resources, including the Florida Department of Transportation, were deployed to assist county officials with road closures, traffic diversions, and infrastructure repairs, noting that severed underground water lines and utility damage affected local residents.
“Look, when you see that video, you know it’s a jarring thing. It was like a missile coming down, and a massive explosion, debris going everywhere, and to have those people on board is really a tragic way to see people pass away,” DeSantis said. “To see the way it descended, I think you can make the inference that something happened in the air that was a big problem.”
Palm Beach County officials ordered precautionary evacuations for roughly 600 residents of a nearby mobile home community affected by emergency closures and utility disruptions. County authorities opened shelters for displaced residents, and the local school district closed nearby John I. Leonard High School on Monday.
Air traffic control recordings captured the flight crew’s reporting icing conditions, moderate turbulence and precipitation before requesting clearance to climb to 37,000 feet. The pilots subsequently declared an emergency as the aircraft began a rapid descent.
In the final transmissions, a crew member reported the aircraft was in an overspeed condition as it descended.
“We are in an overspeed condition descending 20,000 feet per minute,” a crew member radioed before delivering a devastating final transmission: “We’re going to crash into the ground.”
The National Transportation Safety Board launched a specialized “go-team” to lead the inquiry alongside the Federal Aviation Administration. Federal investigators are working to recover the cockpit voice and flight data recorders, review weather radar logs, and examine the aircraft’s maintenance history alongside the flight crew’s type ratings, training, and total hours to determine how the jet entered the fatal dive.

If not corrected, a Mach tuck can lead to a dangerous, rapidly accelerating dive.

sources.news_title: Co-pilot heard screaming before plane crash killed nine is named as 20-year-old
sources.text:
Florida Learjet crash victims named as Texas millionaire, wife and two children
The passengers on board the Learjet 60 which crashed in Florida, killing all nine people on board, have been named - including entrepreneur Adam Robinson, his wife and their young children
A multi-millionaire tech entrepreneur and his young family from Texas have been named among the passengers on the plane which crashed in Florida, killing everyone on board.
Earlier, 20-year-old Nathalia Gadelha was identified by her mother and stepfather as the co-pilot of the Learjet 60 which crashed in Palm Beach County on Sunday afternoon.
The passengers have now been named as entrepreneur Adam Robinson, 44, his wife Helen Sharp, 40, their two children Emma, four, and Charlie, two, their nanny Anita Maria Cetina and two family friends Rachael Reed and Charmi Fehr.
The pilot was identified as 55-year-old Jeff Gregory from Pennsylvania.
All nine people on board were killed when the private jet plunged into a residential neighbourhood in Greenacres before exploding into a fireball. The aircraft had departed Austin-Bergstrom International Airport in Texas and was heading to the Bahamas when it began experiencing problems at around 35,000ft.
Young co-pilot's chilling message to boyfriend
Co-pilot Nathalia sent a message to her boyfriend Justin about ice and turbulence just minutes before the fatal crash, her family revealed earlier.
Her stepfather Thiago Corteleti, 44, told the New York Post: “She texted her boyfriend, I think, at 12:40pm and the accident was at 12:50pm... She just said, 'I’ve got turbulence, I’ve got ice.'”
According to air traffic control recordings, the pilot reported ice building up on the aircraft and turbulence causing sudden changes in altitude. A voice was heard telling controllers: "We have light, clear ice that is manageable and moderate turbulence."
In another desperate transmission, the pilot warned: "We are in an overspeed condition descending 20,000 feet per minute," before adding: "We're going to crash into the ground." Footage captured by witnesses shows the jet banking sharply to the right before plunging to the ground and exploding on impact.
Nathalia, who grew up in Palm Beach County, spoke about her passion for flying in a 2023 interview. She said: “I definitely do brag because people say, ‘Oh, you can’t drive,’ and I’m like, ‘Yeah, but I can fly.'”
She earned her private pilot's licence at just 17, before she even had a driving licence. She began flying lessons in 2020 and also received guidance from her father, who took up flying as a hobby in 2018. Despite being just 20, Nathalia had already clocked up around 1,300 hours of flying experience, according to her family.
Adam Robinson, wife Helen and their children killed
Adam was an entrepreneur who set up tech company Retention. His wife Helen ran communications firm Influential PR and owns a pottery studio, Helen Sharp Ceramics. The family lived in Austin.
Helen's father Dudley Sharp said: "It’s quite a blow. We had a daughter, her husband and two grandchildren on the plane."
Prior to his tech ventures, Adam worked at Lehman Brothers and Barclays Capital according to his LinkedIn profile. He also founded software firm RB2B.
The families of the passengers - including nanny Anita and family friends Rachael and Charmi - released the following statement: "With broken hearts, our families share that Adam Robinson and Helen Sharp, their children Emma and Charlie, Rachael Reed and Charmi Fehr, and Anita Maria Cetina were among those lost aboard the flight that went down near Greenacres, Florida, on November 1.
"Adam and Helen were devoted parents, and Emma, 4, and Charlie, 2, were the light of their lives. Helen and Adam were the love affair that will last forever. Their warmth, generosity and gift for making people feel welcome touched so many lives. Their loss will be felt deeply by all those who loved them and who they loved in return.
"Charmi and Rachel were full of joy and adventure. They loved their people fiercely, fully and without hesitation. From the moment they met, they were all in on each other and the life they were building. They are deeply loved, and we will miss them endlessly.
"Anita Maria cared for Emma and Charlie with tenderness and devotion, and she was truly part of the family. She showed us a legacy of unconditional love and devotion.
"We are deeply grateful to the first responders, investigators, and the Palm Beach County community for their care, and to everyone who has reached out with love. Our hearts are also with the families of the pilots, who are grieving alongside us. We ask for privacy as we grieve."
Plane crash was 'cataclysmic'
Florida Governor Ron DeSantis described the crash as "cataclysmic", adding: "It looked like a missile going down and left a big crater on the side of the road."
Authorities began evacuating around 600 people from a nearby mobile home community following the disaster. Mr DeSantis said there were no immediate reports of anyone on the ground being injured or killed.
Nearby resident Anthony Blackmon told NBC affiliate WTVJ that debris had struck his home. He said: "Debris was everywhere. Debris hit my house. Everything was on fire. The road was on fire."
The cause of the crash remains unclear, with the Federal Aviation Administration and National Transportation Safety Board investigating.

sources.news_title: MichaelSavage.com – PLANE CRASH IN PALM BEACH COUNTY NINE KILLED
sources.text:
Nine people are dead after their Learjet crashed into a mobile home in Greenacres, near Military Trail and North 10th Avenue mid-day Sunday. BocaNewsNow.com broke the story as first responders arrived on the scene. The FAA Sunday afternoon confirmed to BocaNewsNow.com that nine people were on board the Learjet 60 that had departed Austin-Bergstrom International Airport and was en route to North Eleuthera Airport in the Bahamas at the time of the crash. Public tracking data seemingly vanished from airplane tracking services within 30 minutes of the crash. The tail number is registered to a private LLC based in Delaware. The NTSB announced at 5:30 p.m. that is sending a “go team” to the crash scene.
Audio of what is believed to be the crash obtained by BocaNewsNow.com reveals a female pilot in distress as she reports to Air Traffic Control that her plane is descending rapidly, then banking. As the Air Traffic Controller tries to keep her calm, contact is lost. Palm Beach County Fire Rescue took more than an hour to release any information to the public. That led to rumors swirling online that missiles from President Trump’s Mar-a-Lago, just a short distance from the crash site, struck and destroyed the plane. There is no indication — at all — that this rumor is reality, but is seemingly a direct result of Palm Beach County Fire Rescue keeping information private until well after photos, videos, and rumors circulated online. Even as of 3:40 p.m. Sunday, Palm Beach County Fire Rescue has said very little about the crash scene. BocaNewsNow.com learned just a short time after the crash that area hospitals were put on alert for a mass casualty incident. Delray Medical Center, St. Mary’s Medical Center, and Wellington Regional Hospital were all told that a plane crash had occurred and to prepare for multiple victims. The victims never arrived.

sources.news_title: Private jet explodes in deadly crash in Florida – The...
sources.text:
A private Learjet bound for the Bahamas plummeted out of the sky over Palm Beach County, Florida on Sunday afternoon, slammed into the street and exploded, killing all nine people on board and leaving a burning crater in the road.
Video shows the jet diving nose-first toward the ground before it erupted into a ball of fire.
“Debris was everywhere. Debris hit my house. Everything was on fire. The road was on fire,” Anthony Blackmon, who lives near the crash site, told NBC affiliate WTVJ. “I’ve always seen it on the news, never thought it would happen so close to somebody like how it happened today.”
Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis rushed to the scene.
“It was a cataclysmic plane crash,” DeSantis told reporters. “It looked like a missile going down and left a big crater on the side of the road.”
Take a look –
WATCH: New video shows Learjet 60 business jet crashing near West Palm Beach, Florida.
The plane was completely disintegrated upon impact. Number of casualties unknown. pic.twitter.com/l5JT9KEWnQ
— BNO News (@BNONews) November 1, 2026
The jet crashed next to a mobile home community. Authorities evacuated about 600 people from it while federal investigators combed the wreckage.
The $2 million Learjet 60 had taken off from Austin-Bergstrom International Airport in Texas. An airport spokesman described it as a private aircraft. It went down less than eight miles from President Trump’s Mar-a-Lago resort.
The jet was cruising east at 35,000 feet when the trouble started.
The pilot told Miami air traffic controllers that ice was building up on the plane, with an outside temperature of -47 degrees Celsius. Turbulence was throwing the jet up and down by as much as 700 feet, according to recordings captured by LiveATC.net.
Audio from the pilot’s desperate mayday calls have been leaked online. Warning: This is upsetting.
“We’re out of time.” Those may be some of the last words heard from the cockpit of the private jet that plunged into a Florida neighborhood Sunday.
Audio circulating online appears to capture the pilots of the Learjet 60 talking with air traffic control before the crash in… https://t.co/i5n9Gyiq7p pic.twitter.com/74f55yNf5d
— Tony Lane 🇺🇸 (@TonyLaneNV) November 1, 2026
“We’re descending 8,000 — mayday, mayday — we’re descending 10,000 feet per minute,” the pilot radioed.
“We are in an overspeed condition descending 20,000 feet per minute,” the pilot radioed. Then came the final warning: “We’re going to crash into the ground.”
The plane banked hard to the right, then hit the ground and exploded. It had dropped about 27,000 feet in a single minute.
Officials have not released the names of the nine people killed. The New York Post identified the co-pilot as Nathalia Gadelha, a 20-year-old who earned her pilot’s license while still in high school.
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy confirmed the death toll. He called the crash a “horrific tragedy” and said the FAA was sending a team to support the NTSB’s investigation.

sources.text:
Lenny Kravitz’s Rep Debunks Reports He Was Aboard the Learjet 60 That Crashed in Florida
Lenny Kravitz‘s rep is responding to reports that he was aboard the plane that crashed en route to the Bahamas.
If you did not see, a Learjet 60 left Austin-Bergstrom International Airport, headed towards North Eleuthera Airport in the Bahamas on Sunday (November 1) when it crashed in South Florida. All 9 passengers on board were killed.
Why Was Lenny Kravitz Thought to Be on the Airplane That Crashed?
A post on X went viral from a pilot, Emily Shelton, who had announced she was flying with Lenny.
“Honored to be flying the one and only Lenny Kravitz from [Austin-Bergstrom International Airport] to [North Eleuthera Airport, Bahamas] tomorrow. Looking forward to having him on board,” her deleted Facebook post read.
Emily was apparently NOT the pilot on the plane. One of the co-pilots on the plane was Nathalia Gadelha, 20, the New York Post reports.
Lenny Kravitz’s Rep Responds to the Viral Rumor, Revealing He Wasn’t on the Plane
“The reports are untrue and incorrect,” Lenny‘s rep confirmed to BocaNewsNow.
Our thoughts are with the victims and those who lost loved ones in this horrific tragedy.

sources.news_title: Nine people killed after private jet nosedives into residential Florida area
sources.text:
A private jet nosedived and exploded into a fireball beside a residential area in Florida on Sunday, killing all nine people on board.
The violent crash was recorded on multiple dashcams as cars drove incredibly close to the incident on a busy road.
The plane went down right beside Cresthaven, a neighbourhood in Palm Beach County that is just over 10km from Donald Trump’s Mar-a-Lago resort.
It crashed very near the entrance to a mobile home park, with Palm Beach County Commissioner Joel Flores confirming that around 600 residents were evacuated and relocated to shelters.
The crash left a huge crater on the side of the road, with flaming debris recorded inside and around it.
Many passing vehicles could be seen in the vicinity, with locals quick to inspect the destruction.
US transportation secretary Sean Duffy confirmed that all nine people on board the jet were killed in the ‘horrific tragedy’, which occurred at 12.50pm local time.
Florida governor Ron DeSantis said that there were no immediate reports of anyone on the ground injured or killed.
He told reporters: ‘It was a cataclysmic plane crash. It looked like a missile going down and left a big crater on the side of the road.’
The FAA confirmed that the jet had departed Austin Bergstrom International Airport in Texas and was headed for the Bahamas.
Chilling audio from air traffic control revealed that the jet plummeted extraordinarily quickly, dropping hundreds of feet per second.
A person in the cockpit could be heard saying that the plane was ‘picking up precipitation’ and ‘we need to climb’.
Just seconds later, the same voice was raised and declaring that the jet was descending at a rate of 10,000ft (3,048m) per minute.
They then yelled ‘we are in an overspeed condition descending 20,000ft per minute’, and ‘we are going to crash into the ground’.
A mere 35 seconds after the first mayday call was announced, the person said: ‘Holy f***, we’re out of time.’
Palm Beach County Fire Rescue subsequently declared a ‘mass casualty incident’.
Local officials said that the impact of the crash caused considerable damage to local infrastructure, including its water lines, and it would be at least 30 days before the road re-opened.

sources.news_title: Florida plane crash audio reveals harrowing last moments
Co-pilot, 20, who made haunting call before fatal Florida crash is ID'd
sources.text:
THE co-pilot who could be heard pleading for help onboard the doomed Learjet has been identified as a 20-year-old who earned her license in high school.
Nathalia Gadelha Filgueiras was one of nine people who died when a Learjet 60 private plane plummeted over 25,000ft in under a minute before crashing into a residential area in Palm Beach County, Florida, on Sunday.
Filgueiras’ mother, Camila, confirmed to the New York Post that her daughter was co-piloting the twin-engine aircraft when it took off from Austin, Texas, bound for the Bahamas.
The harrowing incident was caught on camera, which showed the private jet nose-diving into the ground and erupting into an enormous fireball.
“It looked like a missile going down. It left a big crater,” Florida Governor Ron DeSantis said.
A chilling audio recorded the cockpit’s final moments before the plane smashed straight into the ground.
Read more in The U.S. Sun
Filgueiras could be heard shouting over the mayday call, “We are in an overspeed condition, descending 20,000ft per minute.”
“We’re descending 8,000 – mayday, mayday, – we’re descending 10,000ft per minute.”
Filgueiras’ male co-pilot and captain, who was identified as Jeff Gregory, 55, was heard reciting the Lord’s Prayer during the distress call.
Gregory is heard saying, “Who are in heaven, hallowed to be the name,” while Filgueiras is heard screaming, “We’re going to crash into the ground.”
Most read in The US Sun
“Holy f**k we’re out of time,” she said before the audio from the Learjet went silent.
The U.S. Sun is choosing not to play the final seconds of the mayday call.
The passengers were identified as tech entrepreneur Adam Robinson, 45, his wife Helen Sharp, 40, and their two children, Emma, 4, and Charlie, 2.
The family was traveling with two close friends, Rachael Reed and Charmi Fehr, and their nanny, Anita Maria Apellido Cetina
The identities of the victims comes after grim rumors spread over the weekend that singer Lenny Kravitz was one of the victims that were onboard the doomed aircraft.
Kravitz’s representative told BocaNewsNow that the reports were “untrue and incorrect.”
Filgueiras, who grew up in Palm Beach County, earned her private pilot’s license in October 2023, as a 17-year-old senior at West Boca Raton High School.
She was featured in a news segment on CBS affiliate WPEC where she revealed she had earned her wings before getting her driver’s license.
“I definitely do brag because people say, ‘Oh, you can’t drive,’ and I’m like, ‘yeah, but I can fly,'” she said at the time.
“I like being different than everyone, so to me, I think it’s cool that like it’s not really an opportunity, I just didn’t do it, and this is how it ended up.
“But I think it’s cool. Some people think that it’s weird that I can fly planes, but I can’t drive a car, I mean I can but, a lot of people think it’s funny.”
Filgueiras started Ground School in 2020 during her sophomore year, but gained firsthand aviation experience from her father who began flying for fun in 2018.
The young pilot explained that she had clocked air miles daily since she entered Ground School, and built 88 hours of flight time on top of passing the knowledge test students need to earn their private pilot’s license.
The Palm Beach County school district paid for Filgueiras’ to get her license through their Aviation Academy.
The National Transportation Safety Board is investigating the crash.
Former pilot Martin Varsavsky theorized that bad weather in the area could have caused the aircraft to fall into a dangerous coffin corner condition.
Coffin corner occurs when a plane’s minimum safe speed and maximum safe speed converge into a narrow range at high altitude, making it difficult to safely fly.
If the plane goes too slow or fast it will stall and rapidly become uncontrollable.
Varsavsky believed the private jet attempted to climb above two storm systems, posting on X, “This accident is very rare, but it follows a pattern similar to that of Air France 447 in 2009, in which more than 200 passengers and crew disappeared in the Atlantic, and to other accidents where the aircraft penetrates or gets too close to the cores of intense storms.
“The radars clearly showed those cells; in light jets, the rule is to deviate with a good margin, not to fly through them—this could be an error by the woman who was piloting.
“What storms do by changing the outside temperature is that airplanes can no longer stay aloft at the same speed.
“It’s called the coffin corner. Or they become very difficult to keep under control.”

sources.news_title: 9 killed as business jet crashes into Florida neighborhood
sources.text:
A business jet crashed into a residential neighborhood in South Florida, killing all nine people aboard and sparking a massive fire, as federal investigators prepared to provide an update Monday on the cause of the crash.
Video recorded by passersby captured the terrifying moment on Sunday afternoon when the Bahamas-bound aircraft plunged from the sky before slamming into the ground and exploding in Green Acres, about 7 miles (11 kilometers) southwest of West Palm Beach. Flames flickered around chunks of pavement lining the crater as shocked residents looked on in horror. Thick black smoke engulfed the crash site.
"Debris was everywhere. Debris hit my house. Everything was on fire. The road was on fire,” Anthony Blackmon, who lives near the crash site, told NBC affiliate WTVJ. "I’ve always seen it on the news, never thought it would happen so close to somebody like how it happened today.”
Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis said there were no immediate reports of anyone on the ground injured or killed. Authorities have not released the names of the people who died.
Palm Beach County authorities were evacuating about 600 people from a nearby mobile home community while the Federal Aviation Administration and National Transportation Safety Board investigate the crash.
Authorities have not provided any information about what caused the Bahamas-bound Learjet 60 to crash. NTSB officials planned to hold a news conference in West Palm Beach on Monday.
The jet began its journey at the Austin-Bergstrom International Airport in Texas, and airport spokesperson Jim Reynolds described it as a private aircraft. He could not immediately provide details about who was on board.
The plane was heading east at 35,000 feet (about 11 kilometers) when the pilot started to report problems.
The pilot said ice was accumulating on the jet and that turbulence was jolting it by as much as 700 feet (213 meters), according to air traffic control recordings captured by LiveATC.net . Rain pounded the region on Sunday.
"We have light, clear ice that is manageable and moderate turbulence,” the pilot told controllers.
The situation rapidly deteriorated.
The pilot requested permission to climb another 2,000 feet (about 610 meters) then quickly declared an emergency as the jet lost altitude at an alarming rate.
"We’re descending 8,000 - mayday, mayday - we’re descending 10,000 feet per minute,” the pilot radioed.
"We are in an overspeed condition descending 20,000 feet per minute,” the pilot radioed, before delivering a devastating acknowledgment of what was about to happen. "We’re going to crash into the ground.”
The plane banked sharply to the right before crashing and exploding.
"It was a cataclysmic plane crash,” DeSantis told reporters at the scene. "It looked like a missile going down and left a big crater on the side of the road.”

sources.news_title: Lenny Kravitz addresses grim rumors he was on doomed Learjet involved in Florida plane crash
sources.text:
Lenny Kravitz addresses grim rumors he was on doomed Learjet involved in Florida plane crash
See more of our coverage in your search results.
Lenny Kravitz clarified that he was not involved in the fatal Florida plane crash on Sunday.
“The reports are untrue and incorrect,” Kravitz’s rep, Carleen Donovan, told BocaNewsNow.
Over the weekend, a Bahamas-bound Learjet crashed into a South Florida mobile home park, killing all nine people on board.
Rumors that the rocker was on the doomed jet went viral on X after a female pilot, wrongly identified as the one flying the doomed $2 million vessel, posted about taking Kravitz on a similar route shortly before the accident.
“Honored to be flying the one and only Lenny Kravitz from [Austin-Bergstrom International Airport] to [North Eleuthera Airport, Bahamas] tomorrow. Looking forward to having him on board,” a screenshot of Florida-based pilot Emily Shelton’s since-deleted Facebook post read.
“’It Ain’t Over ‘Til It’s Over’ is gonna be playing in the cockpit 💃 🎶.”
Fans resurfaced the post on X and immediately assumed that both Shelton and Kravitz had perished in the crash.
Additionally, the 21-year-old pilot had already gone viral in August for making an emergency landing on Interstate 10.
Shelton also spoke out against rumors that she and the Grammy winner were involved in the crash.
“I was recently made aware that there are rumors that I was the pilot of the recent crash in Palm Beach,” she wrote on TikTok Sunday.
Want more celebrity and pop culture news?
Start your day with Page Six Daily.
Thanks for signing up!
“I would like to respectfully clarify I was not. I ask that people please stop speculating and spreading misinformation on this tragedy and be respectful of those involved.
“My heart goes out to all those lost and affected.”
On Monday, The Post exclusively identified the pilot as 20-year-old Nathalia Gadelha, who got her pilot license while still in high school.
The plane, which had departed Austin-Bergstrom International Airport in Texas, took a sharp right turn before nosediving from 8,000 feet into the ground.
Once it crashed, an enormous crater and fireball erupted at the scene.
Authorities have yet to identify the nine people killed in the crash, which Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis called “cataclysmic.”
“It looked like a missile going down, it left a big crater on the side of the road,” he said of the jet.

sources.news_title: Learjet crashes in Florida, killing 9, including female pilot, 20
sources.text:
A Learjet crashed in Palm Beach, Florida, killing 9 passengers and crew on Sunday, Nov. 1. The private jet took off from Austin, Texas and was en route to the Bahamas when it encountered “moderate turbulence” and ice buildup on the wings.
The Learjet flew through thunderstorms in the area before climbing to cruising altitude. The female co-pilot asked an air traffic controller in Miami for permission to climb to 37,000 feet to get above the air turbulence and she was given the green light.
“We’re managing the ice but it is moderate turbulent,” the co-pilot calmly told air traffic control. The co-pilot asked the ATC for “better rides” and the ATC assured her that the ride should improve in Miami’s airspace.
She said the outside temperature was minus 47-degrees Celsius (below zero) at that altitude (-52.6F below zero).
Icing on the wings made it difficult for her to control the craft and the plane began to bank and nosedive. Seconds later, the co-pilot’s tone changed to panic. She told the ATC that the plane was descending rapidly.
“Declaring emergency!” she screamed. “We are in an overspeed condition, descending twenty thousand feet per minute! “We’re going to crash into the ground!”
She continued: “We are descending twenty-two thousand feet (per minute) and we are banking 60-degrees… [screams] Jeff, look outside! Look outside!”
Internet accounts identified the co-pilot as Nathalia Gadelha Filgueiras, 20, and the captain as Jeff Gregory, 55. He is heard reciting the Lord’s Prayer in the cockpit.
The Learjet plunged through the clouds and slammed into the ground around 12:50 p.m. in the area of Military Trail between Cresthaven Boulevard and 10th Avenue North.
Listen to the harrowing audio.
Cell phone footage shows a gaping crater in the roadway and plane debris on fire nearby. According to reports, the plane was a 22-year-old Learjet 60 business jet.
Watch video of the Learjet impacting the ground.
Residents in the neighborhood were forced to evacuate and Military Trail is closed temporarily while the FAA and NTSB investigates the plane crash.
Officials quickly released the audio after conspiracy theorists spread misinformation that the plane was a missile that flew off course.
Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis also said the plane “looked a like a missile” going down. The plane crashed about 9 miles away from President Trump’s Mar-a-Lago estate in Palm Beach.
The Secret Service recently ordered anti-missile defense systems in position around Mar-a-Lago, while the war in Iran continues. The White House already has anti-missile defense systems in place.

sources.news_title: DeSantis Said the Plane Crash Near Mar-a-Lago Looked Like a Missile Hit
sources.text:
Chuck Schumer's government shutdown left air traffic controllers unpaid, furious, and walking off the job.
On Sunday afternoon, a Learjet carrying nine people slammed into a Florida neighborhood nine miles from Mar-a-Lago.
Ron DeSantis stood over the wreckage and said the crater looked exactly like a missile strike.
Learjet 60 Crash in Palm Beach County Leaves Nine Dead Near Mar-a-Lago
The Learjet 60 took off from Austin, Texas, bound for the Bahamas.
It never got there.
Witnesses watched it drop out of the sky over Cresthaven, a quiet Palm Beach County neighborhood, just after 12:50 p.m. Sunday.
It hit the ground nose first and exploded into a fireball.
All nine people on board died instantly.
Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis walked the scene hours later and didn't mince words.
"It looked like a missile going down," he told reporters.
"It left a big crater on the side of the road."
Debris scattered for blocks, displacing roughly 600 residents from a nearby mobile home park.
The Red Cross scrambled to find them somewhere safe to sleep Sunday night.
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy called it a "horrific tragedy" and confirmed the FAA and NTSB are investigating.
Investigators have not said what brought the jet down, and nobody serious is speculating until the black box data comes back.
But the crash lands at a strange moment for American aviation – and conservatives have spent the last year watching exactly why.
The Government Shutdown That Gutted Air Traffic Controllers Was Chuck Schumer's Choice
Go back to October 2025.
Chuck Schumer and Senate Democrats shut down the federal government rather than fund it without their demands.
Air traffic controllers, already working mandatory overtime because the system never recovered from years of Biden-era neglect, got told their paychecks were frozen.
Duffy warned publicly he might have to close off chunks of American airspace if the standoff dragged on.
He called it "mass chaos."
Rep. Garret Graves went further, accusing Schumer directly of turning air traffic controllers into political hostages to win a budget fight.
Rep. Jimmy Patronis said it plainly in a House statement: the Schumer shutdown was putting American transportation at risk.
Controllers didn't wait around to find out what came next.
Call-outs and sick leave spiked as controllers refused to keep working unpaid shifts guiding your family's flight.
Delays and cancellations piled up for weeks, stranding travelers while Schumer held the line in Washington.
That is the system Trump's Department of Transportation inherited – short-staffed, demoralized, and sabotaged by the same party that spent a decade lecturing Republicans about "infrastructure."
Here's what you didn't hear on the evening news.
Duffy didn't just complain about it.
He fixed it.
The FAA brought in a record wave of controller trainees in 2026, racing to rebuild a workforce Washington let rot for years.
The administration rolled out hiring incentives and retention bonuses to keep veteran controllers in the tower instead of walking out the door.
That's not theater.
That's a Transportation Department doing in months what Pete Buttigieg never managed in four years.
Nobody is saying a controller caused Sunday's crash nine miles from the president's own home.
A Learjet 60 going down with no tower anywhere near it points toward mechanical failure or pilot error, the kind investigators spend a year sorting out with engine fragments and cockpit data.
A Learjet 60 did something eerily similar in South Carolina back in 2008, when a blown tire during takeoff sent the jet careening off the runway in a crash that killed four people.
Same aircraft type.
Same sudden, violent end.
The FAA Air Traffic Controller Shortage Is One Shutdown From Happening Again
What this crash does is yank the country's attention back to a system Democrats were willing to gamble with for political leverage one year ago.
Every time a jet goes down anywhere in America right now, people are going to ask whether the person guiding it home had slept, had been paid, or had been pushed out the door by a shutdown Chuck Schumer owns.
That's not fearmongering – that's the direct, predictable consequence of holding federal paychecks hostage over a budget fight.
Duffy and Trump have spent 2026 clawing back the staffing numbers Democrats let collapse, and they deserve credit for treating air traffic control like the national security issue it actually is instead of a bargaining chip.
Nine families are burying someone this week because a plane fell out of the sky in Florida.
But the broader story isn't complicated: Republicans are rebuilding the system that keeps planes in the air, and Democrats are the ones who were willing to break it to win a fight in Washington.

sources.news_title: Federal probe launched into deadly Florida plane crash
A Learjet nosedived into a road, killing 9 on board. Now investigators are probing what caused the ‘cataclysmic plane crash’
sources.text:
(CNN) — In the blink of an eye, a private jet plummeting 450 feet per second nosedived into a Florida roadway, bursting into flames and killing all nine people on board.
“It was a cataclysmic plane crash,” Gov. Ron DeSantis said. “It looked like a missile going down.”
The Learjet 60 was traveling from Austin, Texas, to the Bahamas on Sunday when it plunged from the sky, leaving a massive crater near passing cars in Palm Beach County, Florida. The National Transportation Safety Board said on Monday that one person on the ground had a leg injury. Officials initially said no injuries were reported on the ground.
Authorities have not identified the nine people on board who were killed, but family members have identified eight of the victims.
Adam Robinson, Helen Sharp, and their two children, Emma and Charlie Robinson, have also been identified by family members as being victims, according to a family statement.
CNN has also confirmed through family statements that Rachael Reed, Charmi Fehr and Anita Maria Cetina were on the plane.
The family of 20-year-old Nathalia Gadelha Filgueiras identified her as the plane’s co-pilot.
The NTSB, which will try to determine the cause of the crash, said investigators face significant challenges in piecing together what happened.
“The biggest obstacle that we’re going to have is recovering the major wreckage from the impacted crater on the roadway,” NTSB Senior Air Safety Investigator Tim Monville said.
In addition, “we do have some evidence that there was some breakup of the aircraft before impact. We’re still seeking to determine that,” NTSB Member Tom Chapman said. “We may find some parts of the aircraft some distance from the crash site.”
While the cause of the tragedy remains unknown, air traffic radio captured a pilot’s voice as the plane plunged straight toward the ground.
‘We’re going to crash into the ground!’
Before the crash, Filgueiras reported ice accumulating on the aircraft, with an outside air temperature of -47 degrees Celsius (-53 degrees Fahrenheit), as well as moderate turbulence that bounced the plane by up to 700 feet, according to a recording of air traffic control radio calls captured by LiveATC.net.
But moments later, she shouted, “Mayday, mayday!” in an increasingly panicked voice.
“We’re descending 10,000 feet per minute!” Filgueiras told the Miami Air Route Traffic Control Center.
“We are in an overspeed condition descending 20,000 feet per minute,” she yelled. “We’re going to crash into the ground!”
In reality, the jet plummeted 27,000 feet in one minute, just before flight tracking data was cut off, the website ADS-B Exchange shows.
How ice can accumulate on planes in the sky
The weather conditions are a major focus of the investigation, Chapman said. “What we have to determine is what the weather conditions were like at altitude. They were at about 35,000 feet,” the NTSB official said.
There were scattered storms in the area of the crash, and the plane passed through a stronger storm cell a few minutes before it started plummeting. It is unclear if the storm contributed to the crash.
During the flight, the pilot reported icing, which is one of the biggest weather hazards in aviation.
Icing can cause an increase in weight, a reduction in lift, a decrease in thrust and an increase in drag, according to the Federal Aviation Administration. In other words, icing can slow an aircraft or force it downward.
All clouds at heights where temperatures dip below freezing have the potential to create icing conditions, according to the FAA.
While icing happens more frequently in the winter, it can happen at any time of the year. Even in warm weather, thunderstorms generate powerful updrafts, or columns of rising air that cool rapidly.
The higher the altitude, the colder the air gets. And temperatures in these updrafts can drop to as low as -100 degrees Fahrenheit at the altitudes where planes fly.
Planes are equipped with strong anti-ice systems. But in some cases, the system cannot keep up with the icing.
Ice can “make managing the airplane’s flightpath and airspeed more difficult and can prevent the airplane from maintaining level flight,” the NTSB said.
Ice on wings and other surfaces can pose a major threat to private jets. In January 2024, the NTSB published a safety alert emphasizing the risks of in-flight icing conditions, which can cause pilots to lose control.
Austin family was aboard
Robinson, Sharp and their two children were also victims of the crash on Sunday. Emma was 4 and Charlie was 2.
“It’s quite a blow,” Dudley Sharp, Helen Sharp’s father, told The Palm Beach Post by phone on Monday. “We had a daughter, her husband and two grandchildren on the plane.”
The couple resided in both Aspen, Colorado, and Austin, Texas, where the two had various business ventures. Robinson was a tech entrepreneur who co-founded Robly, an email marketing platform, The Associated Press reported. He also founded Retention.com, a platform that uses technology to connect e-commerce website visitors to their email addresses. Sharp was in the public relations industry and also a ceramics artist.
“Helen and Adam were the love affair that will last forever,” said Robinson’s brother, Anthony, in a family statement shared on Monday. “Their warmth, generosity and gift for making people feel welcome touched so many lives. Their loss will be felt deeply by all those who loved them and who they loved in return.”
In a statement on Instagram, Sharp’s ceramics business said, “She simply radiated.”
Sharp was described as a talented and fun person who loved to travel. She grew up in Houston, went to the University of Arizona and met Robinson in Argentina while living abroad.
“Together, they built a life rooted in family, adventure and love,” the statement read. “Her happiest place was next to Adam and their two beautiful children, along with their dog Bonnie, who was always by her side (and usually in her lap).”
Cetina was identified in the family’s statement as a caregiver for the two children.
“She was truly part of the family,” the statement read. “She showed us a legacy of unconditional love and devotion.”
While it is unclear what the relationship was between Reed, Fehr and the rest of the family, the statement said they were “deeply loved” and will be missed.
Fehr and Reed “were full of joy and adventure. They loved their people fiercely, fully and without hesitation,” the statement read. “From the moment they met, they were all in on each other and the life they were building.”
Co-pilot earned her pilot’s license before her driver’s license
Filgueiras’ family is Brazilian but lives in Florida, where Filgueiras was born, Camila Gadelha Corteleti, her mother, said.
“She was a very good girl – responsible, hardworking,” Corteleti told CNN Brasil. “She was the co-pilot and couldn’t make any decisions.”
No details have been released about the other pilot on board.
Filgueiras received her pilot’s license at age 17, before she even got her driver’s license, her stepfather Thiago Corteleti told CNN Brasil.
The young pilot graduated from American Flyers, one of the most prestigious aviation schools in the United States and had already accumulated more than 1,300 flight hours, her family said.
Filgueiras started ground school in 2020, going into her sophomore year at West Boca Raton High School, CNN affiliate WPEC reported in 2023. She also gained knowledge from her father, who began flying for fun in 2018.
“I like being different than everyone, so to me, I think it’s, like, cool,” Filgueiras told the outlet at the time. “Some people think that it’s, like, weird because I can fly planes, but I can’t drive a car. I mean, I can, but a lot of people think it’s funny.”
The school district paid for Filgueiras to get her private pilot’s license, the station reported. With it, she was able to fly anywhere around the country. Her goal was to become a commercial airplane pilot or fly private jets, the outlet reported.
‘I heard and felt the boom’
The plane hit the ground shortly before 1 p.m. on Military Trail, a major thoroughfare between Cresthaven Boulevard and 10th Avenue North, the Palm Beach County Sheriff’s Office said. The roadway was left shattered and burning wreckage dotted the crater, video from CNN affiliate WPBF showed.
“There is a lot of debris that was strewn as a result of this crash,” DeSantis said.
The scene is just miles from the airport in West Palm Beach that was recently renamed for President Donald Trump and his Mar-a-Lago resort.
About 600 people are in need of shelter because the damage on the ground is blocking the entrance to a mobile home park, said Joel Flores, Palm Beach County commissioner for District 3, who was the first county official at the scene. Residents are being sent to two shelters in the county while the site is being investigated, he said.
“I heard and felt the boom,” Andrew Mannino told CNN. “The power immediately went out and is still out.”
Mannino said he smelled the smoke and saw a large black cloud in the sky.
Sunday’s crash marked the second deadliest plane crash in the US this year, according to NTSB records. In June, 12 people died when a skydiving plane crashed in Butler, Missouri.
The catastrophe is also the deadliest crash involving a Learjet 60, according to data from the Flight Safety Foundation. In 2008, four people were killed when a Learjet 60 bound for Los Angeles crashed on takeoff from Columbia, South Carolina.
Flight data recorder might have been destroyed
Dashcam video showing the crash will be important to investigators piecing together what happened, said Mary Schiavo, CNN aviation analyst and former inspector general for the Department of Transportation.
“That is not a controlled descent,” Schiavo told CNN’s Fredricka Whitfield Sunday. “It’s clear, whatever happened, they had lost control of the plane.”
The steep descent could have forced parts of the plane to break off and the flight data recorder could have been destroyed in the explosion, she added.
Aircraft maintenance records show a cockpit voice recorder was installed on the plane, but it is unclear whether it was still on board, the NTSB said. FAA regulations require jet aircraft with more than one engine to carry a voice recorder if they are flown for hire.
The plane is registered to an LLC in Delaware, according to FAA records, and is listed as available for charter online. It was operated by Aurora Aviation and did business as Upper Jets, according to the NTSB.
Joe Mixon, former NFL running back, posted on X that he flew on that exact Learjet with the same pilots last month. He said he was “absolutely devastated” by the crash.
“Hearing the young woman’s story and learning about the bright future she had ahead of her makes it even more heartbreaking that her life was cut so short,” he wrote in the post.
The NTSB is expected to release a preliminary report within 30 days of the crash. A final report, including the probable causes of the crash, could take one to two years to complete.
CNN Brasil’s Mariana Catacci and CNN’s Cindy Von Quednow, Angela Fritz and Ronnie Glassberg contributed to this report.
