sources.news_title: Nine dead, Florida jet nosedives on busy street near Mar-a-Lago, dashcam shows all, pilot’s bone-chilling final words emerge
sources.text:
THE DAILY BS: HOW MUCH CAN YOU HANDLE?
SPARE ME THE BS (I’ve got things to do)
- All nine aboard a private Learjet died Sunday when it plunged into a Florida neighborhood about nine miles from Mar-a-Lago.
- The pilot reported a terrifying descent of 20,000 feet per minute before warning, “We’re out of time.”
- The crash left a massive crater, forced roughly 600 residents to evacuate and miraculously caused no reported injuries on the ground.
LAY IT ON ME (I’ve got time)
A private jet carrying nine people to the Bahamas plunged out of the South Florida sky Sunday afternoon, exploding into a massive fireball just feet from homes and passing motorists — and leaving behind a chilling recording of the pilot’s final moments.
All nine people aboard were killed.
The Learjet 60 had departed Austin-Bergstrom International Airport in Texas and was headed to North Eleuthera Airport in the Bahamas when something went catastrophically wrong over Palm Beach County.
The aircraft crashed near Military Trail and 10th Avenue North in the Greenacres area, approximately nine miles from President Donald Trump’s Mar-a-Lago estate.
Dashcam footage captured the jet dropping almost vertically before striking the ground and erupting into flames. The impact tore a crater into the pavement and scattered debris across the surrounding neighborhood.
But some of the most disturbing details came from air traffic control recordings.
The pilot had reported encountering icing, turbulence and precipitation and requested a higher altitude.
Then the aircraft began descending at an extraordinary rate.
“We are in an overspeed condition descending 20,000 feet per minute,” the pilot warned controllers.
Moments later came the desperate acknowledgment that the aircraft could not be recovered.
“We’re gonna crash … We’re out of time.”
Those words would be among the final transmissions from the doomed aircraft.
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy confirmed Sunday afternoon that all nine people aboard had died, describing the accident as a “horrific tragedy.”
He asked Americans to pray for the victims’ families and confirmed that the Federal Aviation Administration was assisting the National Transportation Safety Board’s investigation.
Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis visited the scene and described the devastation in stark terms.
“Obviously, this was a cataclysmic plane crash. It looked like a missile going down, it left a big crater on the side of the road,” DeSantis told reporters.
He said debris had been thrown across a considerable distance.
“When you see that video, you know it’s a jarring thing … a massive explosion, debris going everywhere,” the governor said.
The images are difficult to reconcile with the fact that no one on the ground was reported injured or killed.
The aircraft came down close to a busy roadway and the entrance to a mobile-home community. Motorists were passing nearby when the jet struck.
The impact left the community’s main entrance badly damaged, creating immediate problems for residents and emergency crews.
Palm Beach County officials ordered the evacuation of approximately 600 people from the adjacent mobile-home community while investigators examined the wreckage and authorities assessed the surrounding area.
County Commissioner Joel Flores said officials were working to arrange food, shelter and alternative access for displaced residents.
“Right now our priority is evacuating the adjacent community right behind. We have about 600 people that we have to make sure have shelter tonight, food,” Flores said.
Nearby businesses were also expected to remain closed while investigators worked.
Weather conditions are among the circumstances federal investigators will examine.
Heavy rain and thunderstorms were reported in the area around the time of the crash. AccuWeather meteorologist Alan Reppert said the combination of thunderstorms, rainfall and rapidly changing visibility could have created difficult flying conditions.
But investigators have not determined what caused the Learjet to lose control.
The NTSB dispatched a specialized investigative team, with personnel arriving Sunday night and Monday morning. The agency is leading the investigation, supported by the FAA.
Absolutely bone-chilling. https://t.co/neRhckpLNX
— thedailybs w/ Snerdley (@thedailybs_Bo) November 2, 2026
Investigators will examine the aircraft’s flight path, weather conditions, maintenance records, pilot communications and wreckage to determine what happened during the final minutes.
The identities of those killed had not been publicly released in the reporting available early Monday.
The aircraft’s registration was reported as N722BD.
The location of the crash — only miles from Mar-a-Lago — immediately attracted national attention. However, authorities have reported no connection between the flight and the president’s property.
The jet was traveling from Texas to the Bahamas when it encountered trouble over Palm Beach County.
For residents of the neighborhood, the catastrophe unfolded in seconds.
A jet appeared out of the sky, struck the ground with tremendous force and exploded near their homes.
Nine people aboard lost their lives. Hundreds of residents were forced from their homes. And investigators are now tasked with determining how an ordinary flight to the Bahamas ended in one of the most devastating aviation accidents in the area in recent memory.

sources.news_title: Private Jet Crashes into Florida Neighborhood Leaving a Crater and Killing Everyone Onboard
sources.text:
A private jet crashed into Palm Beach County, Florida on Sunday afternoon at such a high speed it left a crater and no traces of the plane. Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis called it “a cataclysmic plane crash” and stated “it looked like a missile was going down.”
According to CNN, the Learjet 60 erupted in a fireball instantly killing all 9 people on board. The pilot detailed ice accumulating on the plane with an air temperature of 047 degree Celsius and turbulence bouncing the plane by 700 feet.
The plane was traveling from Austin, TX to the Bahamas. A frantic pilot could be heard over airwaves. “We’re descending 10,000 feet per minute!”
“We are in an overspeed condition descending 20,000 feet per minute,” they yelled, “We’re going to crash into the ground!”
In total, the plane plummeted at 27,000 feet in one minute before crashing into the ground.

sources.news_title: Jet nosedives and erupts into fireball near busy roadway in West Palm Beach killing all 9 onboard
sources.text:
A business jet carrying nine people nose-dived into a South Florida neighborhood Sunday and erupted into a giant fireball that appeared to just miss homes near a busy roadway. Everyone on board was killed, the nation’s transportation secretary said.
Video recorded by people inside their cars captured the terrifying moment the Bahamas-bound aircraft plunged from the sky before striking near the Palm Beach County roadway and exploding. Flames flickered around chunks of pavement lining a crater as people milled about, expressing shock that it landed only feet from homes and inches from passing vehicles. Thick black smoke engulfed the crash site.
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy posted on X that the Learjet 60 crashed in Palm Beach County at 12:50 p.m. and called it a “horrific tragedy.” The Federal Aviation Administration is sending a team to support the National Transportation Safety Board’s investigation, he said.
Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis said there were no immediate reports of anyone on the ground injured or killed.
“It was a cataclysmic plane crash,” DeSantis told reporters at the scene. “It looked like a missile going down and left a big crater on the side of the road.”
Rain pounded the region on Sunday. A flood watch due to excessive rainfall was in effect through Monday afternoon, the National Weather Service said.
The aircraft had departed Austin-Bergstrom International Airport in Texas and was headed to the Bahamas, according to the Federal Aviation Administration. Authorities did not immediately say what caused the jet to go down or who was on it.
The plane was heading east at 35,000 feet (about 11 kilometers) when pilots reported turbulence, icing and precipitation and requested to climb another 2,000 feet (about 610 meters).
Moments later, the plane entered a steep dive, first 10,000 feet per minute, then 20,000 feet per minute and up to 30,000 feet per minute, speeding the plane beyond its design limits, according to air traffic control recordings and flight tracking data.
A pilot declared an emergency and issued distress calls. The plane banked sharply to the right before it smashed into the ground.
Minutes before the crash, the pilot reported ice accumulating on the jet and turbulence that was jolting it by as much as 700 feet (213 meters), according to air traffic control recordings captured by LiveATC.net.
“We have light, clear ice that is manageable and moderate turbulence,” the pilot told controllers.
But the situation rapidly deteriorated. After encountering precipitation and requesting to climb, the pilot declared an emergency as the aircraft began losing altitude at an alarming rate.
“We’re descending 8,000 – mayday, mayday – we’re descending 10,000 feet per minute,” the pilot radioed.
“We are in an overspeed condition descending 20,000 feet per minute,” the pilot radioed, before delivering a devastating acknowledgment of what was about to happen. “We’re going to crash into the ground.”
Jim Reynolds, a spokesperson for Austin-Bergstrom International Airport, said the jet was a private aircraft. He could not immediately provide details about who was on the flight.
Steve Arroyo, an aviation safety expert, said icing and turbulence could have been factors in the crash and may have caused the plane to stall while it was cruising at 34,000 feet (10,363 meters).
There are many potential factors and the NTSB will consider all of them, including how the pilot responded to the icing and turbulence reported over the radio. But investigators won’t rule anything out at this early stage, he said.
The NTSB said investigators were expected to arrive at the crash site on Sunday and Monday. A media briefing is scheduled for Monday in West Palm Beach.
Palm Beach County authorities were evacuating about 600 people from a nearby mobile home community while federal officials investigate the crash. The road will be closed until further notice, county officials said.
The crash occurred in Greenacres, Florida, according to Palm Beach County sheriff’s officials. The city of 45,000 people is about 7 miles (11 kilometers) southwest of West Palm Beach.

sources.news_title: Florida plane crash kills 9 as investigators probe whether weather played a role
sources.text:
Families identify victims killed in Florida plane crash as investigators probe possible weather link
The plane likely flew through a developing thunderstorm that moved in from the south-east approximately five minutes before the crash, the FOX Forecast Center said.
CRESTHAVEN, Flo. - Families have confirmed the identities of seven of the nine people killed after an airplane crashed into a Florida neighborhood Sunday, as investigators examine whether weather conditions may have contributed to the incident.
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said a Learjet 60 crashed near Cresthaven, Florida, just before 1 p.m. on Sunday. All nine people on board were killed.
The crash left a massive crater on the side of the road and caused significant debris and damage to surrounding infrastructure. In a press conference Sunday, Governor Ron DeSantis said roughly 600 residents are being assisted with temporary shelter and other essential needs.
"This was a cataclysmic plane crash. It looked like a missile going down. It left a big crater on the side of the road," DeSantis said during the press conference.
PRESIDENT TRUMP APPROVES MAJOR DISASTER DECLARATION FOR FLORIDA AFTER HURRICANE ISAIAS
In a statement, the families identified Adam Robinson, Helen Sharp, their children Emma and Charlie, Rachael Reed, Charmi Fehr and Anita Maria Cetina as among those killed. They remembered them as devoted parents, loving family members and joyful friends while thanking first responders and asking for privacy as they grieve.
Investigators are examining whether ice buildup may have played a role in the crash, while preliminary evidence suggests the aircraft may have begun breaking apart before hitting the ground.
In a press conference, Tom Chapman of the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) discussed challenges facing recovery crews, including water accumulating inside the impact crater, which has complicated efforts to retrieve wreckage from the crash site.
HOLIDAY TRAVELERS FACE DECADE-HIGH AIRFARE AS THANKSGIVING AND CHRISTMAS TRIPS GET PRICIER
"There was a lot of debris that was spewed as a result of this crash. As of now, we don't have any reports of anyone who was on the ground apart from the people in the plane who were killed or injured as a result of the debris," DeSantis said.
The plane took off from Austin-Bergstrom International Airport in Austin, Texas, and was headed to North Eleuthera Airport in the Bahamas when it encountered ice and reported turbulence.
Crew reports indicate the pilot asked the air traffic controller for a better ride, and shortly after encountered precipitation.
The FOX Forecast Center said at the surface, both airports reported moderate winds and thunderstorms in the area.
PRESIDENT TRUMP APPROVES MAJOR DISASTER DECLARATION FOR FLORIDA AFTER HURRICANE ISAIAS
"The plane likely flew through a developing thunderstorm that moved in from the south-east approximately five minutes prior to the crash," the FOX Forecast Center said.
The estimated cloud height of the storm was around 44,000 feet — about 7,000 feet higher than the plane was flying. Because of this, it is likely that weather played a role in the crash, the FOX Forecast Center said.
However, it is not 100% certain until officials conduct and finalize their investigation.
WILL THANKSGIVING BRING SNOW, RAIN OR SUNSHINE? FARMERS’ ALMANAC REVEALS ITS 2026 OUTLOOK
Investigators have not yet determined whether the plane was equipped with a flight data recorder, commonly referred to as a black box, which could provide additional information about the moments leading up to the crash.
The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) said the NTSB will handle the investigation.
The NTSB has launched its rapid response team of specialists to investigate the plane crash.
The FOX Forecast Center said a SIGMET warning — an aviation weather advisory alerting pilots to significant, potentially hazardous conditions such as severe thunderstorms and icing — was in effect at the time of the crash.
SEE IT: LARGE CRACK IN GROUND FORMS ON SHOULDER OF ICONIC SOUTHERN CALIFORNIA HIGHWAY
The warning indicated that severe turbulence, in-flight icing and hail were all possible.
Duffy called the crash a "horrific tragedy." Officials have not yet identified the people who died, and the cause of the crash has not yet been determined.
See the families' statements in full below:
A joint statement from the families of Adam Robinson, Helen Sharp, Emma and Charlie Robinson, Rachael Reed, Charmi Fehr and Anita Maria Cetina:
"With broken hearts, our families share that Adam Robinson and Helen Sharp, their children Emma and Charlie, Rachael Reed and Charmi Fehr, and Anita Maria Cetina were among those lost aboard the flight that went down near Greenacres, Florida, on November 1.
Adam and Helen were devoted parents, and Emma, 4, and Charlie, 2, were the light of their lives. Helen and Adam were the love affair that will last forever. Their warmth, generosity and gift for making people feel welcome touched so many lives. Their loss will be felt deeply by all those who loved them and who they loved in return.
Charmi and Rachel were full of joy and adventure. They loved their people fiercely, fully and without hesitation. From the moment they met, they were all in on each other and the life they were building. They are deeply loved, and we will miss them endlessly.
Anita Maria cared for Emma and Charlie with tenderness and devotion, and she was truly part of the family. She showed us a legacy of unconditional love and devotion.
We are deeply grateful to the first responders, investigators, and the Palm Beach County community for their care, and to everyone who has reached out with love. Our hearts are also with the families of the pilots, who are grieving alongside us.
We ask for privacy as we grieve. Details about memorial services will be shared once arrangements are made."
Retention.com, RB2B, and Moltsets Team Statement
"We are heartbroken by the loss of Adam Robinson, our CEO and co-founder, his wife Helen and their two young children, who died in a tragic plane crash in Palm Beach County, Florida, on November 1, 2026.
Adam was much more than our CEO. He was a friend, a mentor and a bold, outspoken leader who lived life to the fullest. He cared deeply about the people around him and brought energy and conviction to everything he built. His loss is deeply felt across our team and the tech community, as we collectively mourn this significant loss.
Our hearts are with Adam and Helen’s family and loved ones, and with everyone affected by the crash. We ask that their privacy be respected during this difficult time.
Our immediate focus at Retention.com, RB2B, and Moltsets is supporting our employees and Adam and Helen’s family. We are grateful for the kindness and support extended to them and our team."

sources.news_title: Deadly Learjet Crash Kills All Nine Aboard
sources.text:
AUTOMATED SUMMARY
A Learjet 60 business jet carrying nine people crashed in Greenacres, Palm Beach County, Florida, on Sunday after leaving Austin, Texas, for the Bahamas. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said all nine people aboard were killed.

sources.news_title: Nine killed after Learjet 60 plunges into Florida neighborhood; crew reported severe icing before final transmission
sources.text:
The Briefing:
- A 22-year-old Learjet 60 carrying nine people nosedived into a residential neighborhood near Greenacres, Palm Beach County, Florida, on Sunday, killing all nine on board and leaving no ground casualties.
- Minutes before impact, the crew radioed reports of severe icing and turbulence before a crew member's voice broke over the frequency with a chilling final message: "We're going to crash into the ground."
- The National Transportation Safety Board is leading the federal investigation; approximately 600 residents near the crash site were evacuated as authorities secured the area.
A private Learjet 60 on a charter flight from Austin, Texas, to the Bahamas turned into a catastrophe over suburban Palm Beach County on Sunday, November 1, when the aircraft entered an uncontrolled nosedive and struck the ground at approximately 12:50 p.m. ET. All nine people aboard perished. No injuries were reported at ground level.
The jet — a twin-engine business aircraft registered as N722BD, 22 years old at the time of the crash — went down near Military Trail between Cresthaven Boulevard and 10th Avenue North in Greenacres, a dense residential corridor just miles south of what is now officially named President Donald J. Trump International Airport, formerly Palm Beach International Airport.
"We're Going to Crash Into the Ground"
Air traffic control recordings document a cockpit crew losing command of the aircraft with terrifying speed. The plane was cruising at 35,250 feet and 437 knots when the pilots radioed reports of icing, precipitation, and violent jolts, simultaneously requesting clearance to ascend an additional 2,000 feet. That request became irrelevant almost instantly.
The FAA confirmed the aircraft dropped from 35,250 feet to 8,750 feet in just over a minute — a descent rate the agency calculated at roughly 350 feet per second, well beyond the structural tolerance of the airframe. One crew member's voice pierced the frequency in the final seconds with a haunting transmission: "We're going to crash into the ground."
Fireball Tears a Crater Into Military Trail
Dashcam and cellphone footage from passing motorists captured the Learjet in an almost-vertical plunge before a violent explosion lit the afternoon sky over Greenacres. The impact gouged a deep crater into the roadway near the entrance to a mobile home community and a strip mall at 3001 South Military Trail, sending thick black smoke visible for miles in every direction.
Florida Governor Ron DeSantis, who traveled to the scene in person, described watching the footage and said the plane "appeared like a missile" coming down, labeling the event "cataclysmic." Palm Beach County authorities evacuated approximately 600 residents from the surrounding mobile home community as federal investigators began arriving on scene. Despite the severity and proximity to homes, no ground casualties were immediately reported.
NTSB Dispatches Go-Team; Cause Remains Unknown
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy confirmed all nine deaths via social media, calling Sunday's crash "a horrific tragedy" and noting that the FAA had dispatched a support team. The NTSB confirmed it was sending a full go-team to the site, with investigators expected to arrive through Sunday night and into Monday. A formal media briefing is scheduled in West Palm Beach on Monday.
Investigators have not yet publicly named those aboard or formally identified a probable cause. The icing and turbulence captured in the final transmission are expected to dominate the early phase of the inquiry, alongside a close review of the jet's maintenance records and the flight crew's decisions during the plane's final minute. A preliminary NTSB report is expected within 30 days.
Second-Deadliest U.S. Aviation Accident of 2026
Sunday's crash is the deadliest aviation accident on American soil since a PAC P-750 skydiving plane went down shortly after takeoff near Butler, Missouri, on June 14, 2026, killing all 12 people aboard. The Greenacres disaster now ranks as the second-deadliest aviation accident in the United States this year.
The Learjet 60, a mid-size business jet built by Bombardier and widely used across the private charter industry, has logged decades of commercial service. Whether the specific airframe's condition or maintenance history played any role in Sunday's catastrophe will stand as one of the central questions federal investigators must answer in the weeks ahead.

WATCH | Learjet crashes in Florida, nine dead
Nine people died when a private jet plunged into a Florida neighbourhood. Disturbing details have emerged about the aircraft’s final moments.
Nine people have died after a private Learjet crashed into a residential neighbourhood in Florida, United States, on Sunday, 1 November.
The Learjet 60 was travelling from Austin, Texas, to the Bahamas when it plunged into the ground near a busy road in Palm Beach County shortly before 13:00 local time.
All nine people on board died.
Videos circulating on social media show the aircraft descending almost vertically before striking the ground and erupting into a massive fireball.
The impact left a large crater near a mobile home park, with debris scattered across the surrounding area.
Pilot’s chilling final words
According to reports, air traffic control recordings captured the pilot reporting ice accumulation, turbulence and heavy precipitation shortly before the crash.
The crew requested permission to climb to a higher altitude in search of better flying conditions.
However, the situation deteriorated rapidly.
The pilot declared an emergency as the aircraft began losing altitude at an alarming rate, reportedly exceeding 32 000 feet per minute at one point.
In the final moments, the pilot warned controllers that the aircraft was heading towards the ground.
The last words heard from the cockpit were: “We’re out of time.”
Hundreds evacuated after crash
Florida Governor Ron DeSantis described the crash as a major tragedy, comparing the aircraft’s final descent to a missile striking the ground.
About 600 residents living near the crash site were evacuated, with authorities arranging temporary shelter.
There were no immediate reports of deaths or injuries on the ground.
US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy confirmed the nine fatalities and extended his condolences to the victims’ families.
The identities of those killed have not yet been released.
The National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB), assisted by the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), has launched an investigation.
Although the crew reported icing and turbulence, investigators have not established what caused the aircraft to crash.

sources.news_title: 'We're Out of Time' — Chilling Audio from Cockpit of Tragic Learjet Reveals Pilot's Final Words before Fireball Crash near Donald Trump's Mar-a-Lago Resort
sources.text:
'We're Out of Time' — Chilling Audio from Cockpit of Tragic Learjet Reveals Pilot's Final Words before Fireball Crash near Donald Trump's Mar-a-Lago Resort
Nov. 2 2026, Published 7:27 a.m. ET
Chilling audio footage has been released from the doomed Learjet flight moments before its fireball crash in Florida.
RadarOnline.com can reveal the recording captured the pilot’s terrified voice as the private jet dived out of the sky and into the ground at a mobile home park, close to Donald Trump's Mar-A-Lago estate, killing all nine on board.
'We're Going To Crash Into The Ground'
The pilot reported to air traffic control (ATC) the jet was "going to crash into the ground" before screaming, "We're descending 8,000. Mayday. Mayday. We're descending 10,000ft per minute."
Seconds later, another communication with ATC heard the pilot say: "Declaring emergency. We are in an overspeed condition descending 20,000ft per minute.
"We're going to crash into the ground."
Heartbreakingly, she then says in her final words that the jet is "descending at 22,000ft. Look outside. We're going to die. Holy f---, we're out of time."
Prior to Sunday’s tragic crash, the pilot had reported "moderate turbulence" and that the temperature was -47C as well as rain.
'Massive Explosion'
"We're managing the ice but it is moderate turbulence," she says, with ATC chillingly telling her to expect "better rides ahead".
The $2million Learjet 60 traveling from Texas crashed near the intersection of Military Trail and 10th Avenue North.
Harrowing dash camera footage showed the jet sharply crashing to the ground and causing the massive explosion.
Speaking at the crash site, Governor Ron DeSantis said: "When you see that video, you know, it's a jarring thing.
'It Was Like A Missile Coming Down'
'It was like... a missile coming down and a massive explosion, debris going everywhere.'
The impact left debris scattered across a significant distance and a massive crater in the road, but authorities said nobody on the ground was injured or killed in the crash.
A local resident gave her account of the disaster to Fox News, saying: “It felt like a super big explosion.”
“There was like some smoke, black smoke,' the resident added. 'And then we started hearing... the sirens sounding three minutes after.'
Other witnesses have described being 'lifted from the ground' as the road started to buckle and a massive blaze erupted.
Yet nearly 600 residents of a nearby mobile home community are now being forced to relocate, with authorities saying the entrance to their neighborhood was located directly next to the wreckage.
"Unfortunately, that's a crime scene. They're investigating that, so the people can't stay there," former Greenacres Mayor and current Palm Beach County Commissioner Joel Flores said at a news conference.
The crash also damaged nearby infrastructure, potentially affecting water and other services, he and other elected officials said.
Meanwhile, it remains unlikely that the part of the road where the plane crashed will be open "in the next 30 days," Flores said.
Nearby businesses may also face prolonged closures as crews work to repair the roadway and federal investigators from the National Transportation Safety Board examine the wreckage.
The cause of the crash remains unclear.

sources.news_title: 'We're Out of Time': Learjet Crash Kills 9 in Florida
sources.text:
A private jet carrying nine people nose-dived into a road beside a mobile home community in Palm Beach County, Florida, on Sunday afternoon and exploded in a fireball that witnesses compared to a missile strike, killing everyone on board and leaving a crater at the edge of one of the county's busiest commercial corridors. No one on the ground was hurt, Gov. Ron DeSantis said, but roughly 600 residents of the neighboring mobile home park were evacuated while federal investigators secured the wreckage, and the road was closed indefinitely.
The aircraft, a 22-year-old twin-engine Learjet 60 registered N722BD, had departed Austin-Bergstrom International Airport in Texas at about 10:37 a.m. Central time bound for North Eleuthera Airport in the Bahamas, the Federal Aviation Administration said. It came down at 12:50 p.m. Eastern near Military Trail between Cresthaven Boulevard and 10th Avenue North, in the Greenacres area west of West Palm Beach, after what the FAA described as a rapid descent of about 350 feet per second. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy confirmed on X that all nine people aboard had died. The airport's spokesman in Austin, Jim Reynolds, said the jet was a private aircraft and that he could not immediately say who was on it. Authorities had not released the names of the dead by Monday morning.
The last moments were recorded. Air traffic control audio captured a series of distress calls from the cockpit as the jet lost altitude, ending with the pilot telling the tower: "We're gonna crash. We're out of time." Video from the ground showed the aircraft dropping almost vertically out of a grey sky and erupting in flame on impact, the plume of black smoke visible across the county. "Everything was on fire," one resident said. Another, Roger Forcelle, said he had felt the aircraft pass low over his house seconds before the explosion.
DeSantis, who went to the scene on Sunday, did not soften the description. "It was a cataclysmic plane crash," he told reporters. "It looked like a missile going down and left a big crater on the side of the road." He said no residents or motorists had been injured, which given the location, a strip of roadway lined with shops and homes on a Sunday afternoon, was the one piece of fortune in the day. At least one mobile home appeared to have been damaged in the impact, and Palm Beach County Fire Rescue initially declared a mass casualty incident before it became clear that the casualties were confined to the aircraft.
The weather was the first variable investigators flagged. Rain pounded South Florida for most of Sunday, with thunderstorms in the Palm Beach area around the time of the crash, visibility reported at between two and 10 miles and wind gusts of 20 to 30 mph, and the National Weather Service had a flood watch for excessive rainfall in effect through Monday afternoon. Whether the conditions contributed, and whether the jet was attempting a diversion or an emergency landing at Palm Beach International, which lies a few miles to the northeast, has not been established. The FAA's description of a 350-foot-per-second descent, roughly 21,000 feet per minute, is far beyond anything a controlled approach would produce and suggests the aircraft was either out of control or in a deliberate steep dive in its final seconds. The distress calls indicate the crew knew it was in trouble before the end.
The National Transportation Safety Board said Sunday it was launching a go-team, with investigators arriving Sunday evening and Monday morning and a media briefing scheduled for Monday in West Palm Beach. The early work, the board said, would focus on recovering the wreckage, reviewing air traffic control recordings and examining the weather. The FAA is sending its own team to support the inquiry. A Learjet 60 of this generation is typically fitted with a cockpit voice recorder, and investigators will be looking for it in debris that was still being cooled on Sunday night. A preliminary report normally follows within about 30 days; a probable cause can take a year or more.
The Learjet 60 is a mid-size business jet built by Bombardier's Learjet division in Wichita, Kansas, between the early 1990s and the late 2000s, seating up to eight passengers behind two pilots. It is a common aircraft on the Florida–Bahamas run, a flight of under an hour from the Palm Beach coast, and North Eleuthera is a frequent destination for private aircraft serving the resort communities of Harbour Island and the island's northern settlements. An aircraft of this age, if it was on a private rather than charter certificate, would operate under less demanding maintenance and crew-rest rules than a commercial carrier, a distinction the NTSB routinely examines in business-jet accidents.
The crash is the deadliest aviation accident in Florida this year and the latest in a run of general-aviation disasters that has put the sector under scrutiny. Palm Beach County has its own history: in October 2015 a small plane fell into the Mar-Mak Colony Club mobile home park in nearby Palm Springs, killing people on the ground as well as aboard, and the proximity of Sunday's impact to another mobile home community, with hundreds of residents evacuated and homes on the edge of the crater, underlined how narrowly a worse outcome was avoided.
For the families of the nine, the next days will be spent waiting on identifications that the intensity of the fire will complicate, and on the first factual account from the NTSB. For the hundreds displaced from their homes on Sunday, the question is when the road reopens and the wreckage is cleared. And for investigators, the sequence that matters begins somewhere over the Gulf of Mexico or the Florida peninsula, when a routine two-hour flight to a Bahamian beach airport became, in the pilot's own words, a crash the crew could see coming and could not stop.

sources.news_title: Jet crashes into Florida neighborhood, killing all 9 aboard
sources.text:
By Amy Taxin
Associated Press
PALM BEACH COUNTY, Fla. — A business jet carrying nine people nose-dived into a South Florida neighborhood Sunday and erupted into a giant fireball that appeared to just miss homes near a busy roadway. Everyone on board was killed, the nation’s transportation secretary said.
Video recorded by people inside their cars captured the terrifying moment the Bahamas-bound aircraft plunged from the sky before striking near the Palm Beach County roadway and exploding. Flames flickered around chunks of pavement lining a crater as people milled about, expressing shock that it landed only feet from homes and inches from passing vehicles. Thick black smoke engulfed the crash site.
| MORE: A simple MCI tabletop exercise
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy posted on X that the Learjet 60 crashed in Palm Beach County at 12:50 p.m. and called it a “horrific tragedy.” The Federal Aviation Administration is sending a team to support the National Transportation Safety Board’s investigation, he said.
Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis said there were no immediate reports of anyone on the ground injured or killed.
“It was a cataclysmic plane crash,” DeSantis told reporters at the scene. “It looked like a missile going down and left a big crater on the side of the road.”
Rain pounded the region on Sunday. A flood watch due to excessive rainfall was in effect through Monday afternoon, the National Weather Service said.
The aircraft had departed Austin-Bergstrom International Airport in Texas and was headed to the Bahamas, according to the Federal Aviation Administration. Authorities did not immediately say what caused the jet to go down or who was on it.
The plane was heading east at 35,000 feet (about 11 kilometers) when pilots reported turbulence, icing and precipitation and requested to climb another 2,000 feet (about 610 meters).
Moments later, the plane entered a steep dive, first 10,000 feet per minute, then 20,000 feet per minute and up to 30,000 feet per minute, speeding the plane beyond its design limits, according to air traffic control recordings and flight tracking data.
A pilot declared an emergency and issued distress calls. The plane banked sharply to the right before it smashed into the ground.
Minutes before the crash, the pilot reported ice accumulating on the jet and turbulence that was jolting it by as much as 700 feet (213 meters), according to air traffic control recordings captured by LiveATC.net.
“We have light, clear ice that is manageable and moderate turbulence,” the pilot told controllers.
But the situation rapidly deteriorated. After encountering precipitation and requesting to climb, the pilot declared an emergency as the aircraft began losing altitude at an alarming rate.
“We’re descending 8,000 – mayday, mayday - we’re descending 10,000 feet per minute,” the pilot radioed.
“We are in an overspeed condition descending 20,000 feet per minute,” the pilot radioed, before delivering a devastating acknowledgment of what was about to happen. “We’re going to crash into the ground.”
Jim Reynolds, a spokesperson for Austin-Bergstrom International Airport, said the jet was a private aircraft. He could not immediately provide details about who was on the flight.
Steve Arroyo, an aviation safety expert, said icing and turbulence could have been factors in the crash and may have caused the plane to stall while it was cruising at 34,000 feet (10,363 meters).
There are many potential factors and the NTSB will consider all of them, including how the pilot responded to the icing and turbulence reported over the radio. But investigators won’t rule anything out at this early stage, he said.
The NTSB said investigators were expected to arrive at the crash site on Sunday and Monday. A media briefing is scheduled for Monday in West Palm Beach.
Palm Beach County authorities were evacuating about 600 people from a nearby mobile home community while federal officials investigate the crash. The road will be closed until further notice, county officials said.
The crash occurred in Greenacres, Florida, according to Palm Beach County sheriff’s officials. The city of 45,000 people is about 7 miles (11 kilometers) southwest of West Palm Beach.

WILMINGTON, Del. (WPVI) -- The private plane that crashed in Florida while heading to the Bahamas was registered to an LLC based in Wilmington, Delaware, according to the United States Department of Transportation.

NTSB is documenting known parts that have been found at the scene, as well as interviewing witnesses.
Officials say if someone finds debris, do not move it and call 911 to report it.
The FAA will assist the NTSB with its investigation.

sources.news_title: 20-year-old co-pilot killed in Florida Learjet crash earned pilot's license in high school
sources.text:
20-year-old co-pilot killed in Florida Learjet crash earned pilot's license in high school
GREENACRES, Fla. (CBS12) — The co-pilot aboard the Learjet that crashed in a fiery explosion in Palm Beach County on Sunday has been identified as a young aviator who earned her pilot's license while still in high school, according to her family.
On Monday, the co-pilot's family identified her as 20-year-old Nathalia Filgueiras. According to her family, Filgueiras was co-piloting a Learjet 60 from Austin, Texas, to the Bahamas when the aircraft began to plummet and crashed on South Military Trail between Cresthaven Boulevard and 10th Avenue in Greenacres.
CBS12 News interviewed Filgueiras in 2023 after she earned her private pilot's license before getting her driver's license at age 17 while attending West Boca Raton High School.
During the interview, Filgueiras said she began ground school in 2020 and had also learned about aviation from her father, who started flying recreationally in 2018.
Filgueiras had logged 88 flight hours before earning her private pilot's license in 2023.
Filgueiras died Sunday afternoon with eight others in the fiery plane crash that killed all nine people on board.
The crash happened around 12:50 p.m. on South Military Trail between Cresthaven Boulevard and 10th Avenue North. Flames erupted along the roadway as thick smoke billowed into the sky. Witnesses reported hearing a loud boom that could be heard for miles.
The crash occurred near several businesses. County officials said no one on the ground was injured, but about 600 residents of a nearby mobile home park were evacuated and relocated to shelters.

sources.text:
A small twin-engine business aircraft crashed into a suburban South Florida neighborhood on Sunday, killing all nine individuals on board and sending a plume of heavy fire and smoke over the crash site. Federal and local emergency officials confirmed that the Learjet 60 had departed from Austin-Bergstrom International Airport in Texas and was en route to North Eleuthera Airport in the Bahamas when it violently went down in Greenacres, located within Palm Beach County. Authorities have not publicly identified the victims aboard the charter flight.
According to flight-tracking platform ADS-B Exchange, the twin-engine jet suddenly began an extreme dive over West Palm Beach, plunging approximately 27,000 feet in just sixty seconds prior to signal termination. Air traffic control communications captured distress transmissions from the cockpit shortly before impact, with the pilot calling out, “We’re descending 8,000 – mayday, mayday – we’re descending 10,000 feet per minute,” followed by, “We are in an overspeed condition descending 20,000 feet per minute … We’re going to crash into the ground.”
The aircraft struck a suburban thoroughfare along South Military Trail near Cresthaven Boulevard, buckling the asphalt and carving out a smoldering crater near a mobile home community. First responders swarmed the scene to extinguish the flames and secure the area, resulting in the full closure of Military Trail between Cresthaven Boulevard and 10th Avenue North. Authorities confirmed that emergency crews worked through the afternoon to assess ground damage, with no ground casualties or fatalities verified as of late Sunday.
“Today’s plane crash in Palm Beach County, Florida is a horrific tragedy,” Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said in a statement released on social media Sunday. Weather monitoring stations in the surrounding area reported active thunderstorms, lightning, and wind gusts approaching 25 mph around the time of the incident. Data indicates the jet traversed a severe weather cell moments before entering its steep descent, though investigators noted it remains unclear whether atmospheric conditions played a direct role in the catastrophe.
The National Transportation Safety Board and the Federal Aviation Administration have formally initiated a joint investigation to determine the precise cause of the accident. Federal investigators expect to remain at the impact site over the coming days to collect wreckage, evaluate flight recorder data, and analyze atmospheric conditions present during the flight path.

By Julie Ingwersen
CHICAGO, Nov 1 (Reuters) – A Learjet crashed on Sunday afternoon in a residential area in Palm Beach County, Florida, killing all nine people on board, US transportation officials said.
The private jet had taken off from Austin-Bergstrom International Airport in Texas and was headed to North Eleuthera Airport in the Bahamas, the Federal Aviation Administration said in a statement.
Videos on social media showed the jet slamming into the ground next to a road and exploding.
“It was a big-time tragedy that happened,” Florida Governor Ron DeSantis said at a press conference near the crash site in Lake Worth Beach. “When you see that video, it’s a jarring thing. It was like a missile coming down, and a massive explosion, debris going everywhere.”
The National Transportation Safety Board said it had launched an investigation into the crash, which Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy called a “horrific tragedy.”
FAA records list the Bombardier-made Learjet 60’s owner as a Delaware corporation. Canada-based Bombardier said it would fully support the investigation and cooperate as needed.
The crash left a “massive crater” by the road near the entrance to a mobile home park, Palm Beach County Commissioner Joel Flores said at the news conference. About 600 people were being evacuated from the area and relocated to two shelters in the county, Flores said.
Heavy rainfall and thunderstorms were occurring in the area at the time, forecaster AccuWeather said in a statement.
An audio recording from a Miami air traffic control center posted on LiveATC, a site that broadcasts air traffic control communications, captured the plane’s final moments before the crash in unusual detail.
At first, someone in the plane’s cockpit reported to an air traffic controller that they were “managing the ice” but faced “moderate” turbulence and were seeking “better rides”.
Less than a minute later, the person said “Mayday, mayday,” reporting that the plane was suddenly descending at a rate of 10,000 feet per minute.
Seconds later, the person said they were declaring an emergency, with the rate of descent accelerating to 20,000 feet per minute.
Less than 20 seconds later, the person said: “We’re going to crash into the ground” before saying that the descent rate had reached 22,000 feet per minute as the plane started banking.
About 35 seconds after the initial mayday announcement, the last thing heard from the cockpit was a rapidly spoken “We’re out of time.”
Flight tracking website Flightradar24 said data showed the vertical descent rate at one point exceeded 32,000 feet per minute.

sources.news_title: Weather could have played a role in deadly Florida jet crash, aviation expert says
sources.text:
Weather could have played a role in deadly Florida jet crash, aviation expert says
GREENACRES, Fla. (WPEC) — The lack of recognizable wreckage at the scene of Sunday's fiery Learjet crash in Greenacres could be the result of a high-speed impact, according to an aviation expert who also raised questions about whether thunderstorms played a role in the aircraft's rapid descent.
DeWitt Ingram, a Learjet type-rated captain and founder and president of Par-Avion Group Aviation Consulting, reviewed flight-tracking information and videos showing the aircraft's final moments.
He reviewed flight-tracking information and videos showing the aircraft’s final moments.
“It’s a very sad day in aviation,” Ingram said.
The Learjet 60 crashed near Military Trail and 10th Avenue North.
FlightRadar24 lists its route from Austin, Texas, to North Eleuthera in the Bahamas.
The path shows the aircraft crossing the Gulf before entering Florida near Naples. It continued northeast across the state, then curved south over Palm Beach County.
Ingram said the flight’s rapid descent raised immediate questions.
According to his review, the aircraft had flown at approximately 41,000 feet before descending to 35,000.
He said it then descended from approximately 35,000 feet to the ground in about one minute.
“What we saw today is a jet coming out of high altitude very quickly,” Ingram said.
Weather among the questions
Ingram said thunderstorms could have exposed the aircraft to powerful air currents and severe turbulence.
He questioned whether those conditions upset the aircraft’s flight path, potentially causing a loss of control.
“If the pilot flew into the tops of one of the thunderstorms, in that very rough air, he could have damaged the airplane to the point where he lost control,” Ingram said.
He explained that an uncontrolled descent could increase speed and place excessive stress on the aircraft.
However, whether this aircraft encountered those conditions remains unconfirmed. Weather-related damage and an in-flight breakup also have not been established.
The flight path alone does not explain why the aircraft turned or descended.
Why little recognizable wreckage may be visible
Images from the scene prompted questions about why large aircraft sections were not clearly visible.
Ingram said a high-speed impact can shatter an aircraft into small fragments.
“The energy transfer breaks apart the aircraft fuselage,” he said.
That could explain why viewers do not see an intact tail or recognizable cabin.
He said heavier parts, such as engine components and landing gear, may remain.
A sad day close to home
Ingram said he was nearby when his niece contacted him about a loud explosion.
She told him the power had gone out where she lived.
He then looked toward the area and saw a dark cloud rising from the crash.
For Ingram, the scene brought both personal sadness and professional questions.
The cause remains unconfirmed. His analysis offers possible explanations for investigators to examine, including weather and a loss of control.

sources.text:
A private Learjet 60 crashed in a residential area of Palm Beach County, Florida, killing all nine people on board, after reporting ice and turbulence during its flight to the Bahamas.

The aircraft manufacturer, Bombardier, said it would cooperate fully with investigators. The identities of the nine people killed had not been publicly released as of Monday.

sources.text:
Learjet Bound for the Bahamas Nose-Dives Into Florida Neighborhood, All 9 Aboard Killed
A private jet carrying nine people plunged out of the sky into a Palm Beach County, Fla., neighborhood Sunday afternoon and burst into a fireball, killing everyone on board.
The Learjet 60 crashed at about 12:50 p.m. near Military Trail and 10th Avenue North near Greenacres, the Federal Aviation Administration said. It had left Austin-Bergstrom International Airport in Texas and was headed to North Eleuthera Airport in the Bahamas, WPTV reported.
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy confirmed all nine people aboard were killed, calling the crash a “horrific tragedy.”
“Please join me in praying for the families and loved ones of those we lost,” Duffy said.
Feet From Homes, Inches From Cars
Video shot from passing cars captured the jet nose-diving and exploding near the roadway, leaving flames flickering around chunks of pavement in a crater, the Associated Press reported. Onlookers expressed shock that it came down only feet from homes and inches from passing vehicles. A woman working nearby said the power had been out for about two hours.
As of 4 p.m., officials had not confirmed any deaths on the ground, USA Today reported. Weather at the time was overcast with rain and lightning in the area and east winds gusting to near 25 mph, according to the National Weather Service in Miami.
The crash site is about nine miles from Mar-a-Lago, President Donald Trump’s Palm Beach resort, the BBC reported. Palm Beach County Fire Rescue declared a mass casualty incident.
NTSB Takes the Lead
The National Transportation Safety Board will lead the investigation, with an FAA team assisting. Authorities have not said what caused the crash or who was aboard. An airport spokesman said the tail number was N722BD, and registration records show the plane belongs to LR60271 LLC, a Wilmington, Del., company, CBS12 reported.
The Palm Beach County Sheriff’s Office closed Military Trail in both directions between Cresthaven Boulevard and 10th Avenue North and asked drivers to avoid the area.

Nine die after a Learjet erupts into flames in Florida air crash
CHICAGO — Nine people were killed after a Learjet crashed and erupted in a fireball on Sunday afternoon in a residential area in Palm Beach County, Florida, US transportation officials said.
The private jet had taken off from Austin-Bergstrom International Airport in Texas and was headed to North Eleuthera Airport in the Bahamas, the Federal Aviation Administration said in a statement.
Videos on social media showed the jet slamming into the ground next to a road and exploding
The crash is the second deadliest in the United States this year, according to National Transportation Safety Board records, following June’s skydiving plane crash in Butler, Missouri, which killed 12.
Officials have not identified the nine people who were aboard the plane or said how many were passengers and crew.
“It looked like a missile going down,” Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis said of the crash.
There are no reports of anyone on the ground being killed, but the crash did create a significant debris field, the governor said.
About 600 people are in need of shelter on the ground because the crash scene is blocking the entrance to a mobile home park and residents can’t stay there, a county official said.
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy, who confirmed the deaths, called the crash a “horrific tragedy.”
The Federal Aviation Administration and NTSB will investigate the crash, the FAA said.
NTSB investigators will arrive at the site Sunday and Monday. A news conference is also planned for Monday.
Sunday’s incident is the worst crash involving a Learjet 60, according to data from the Flight Safety Foundation. In 2008, four people were killed when a Learjet 60 bound for Los Angeles crashed on takeoff from Columbia, South Carolina.
The Learjet 60 was flying to the Bahamas from Austin-Bergstrom International Airport, according to the FAA. It is registered to an LLC in Delaware, according to FAA records, and is listed as available for charter online.
Learjets are synonymous with private flying. Bill Lear’s iconic Lear 23 caught on with the rich and famous shortly after its introduction in the 1960s. The brand was most recently made by Canadian manufacturer Bombardier. The company discontinued making new Learjets in 2021, but continues to support them.
Minutes before the crash, the pilot of the plane reported ice accumulating on the aircraft, an outside air temperature of -47 degrees Celsius, and moderate turbulence, bouncing the plane by up to 700 feet, according to a recording of air traffic control radio calls captured by LiveATC.net.
“We have light, clear ice that is manageable and moderate turbulence,” the pilot radioed the Miami Air Route Traffic Control Center.
Minutes before the crash, the pilot of the plane reported ice accumulating on the aircraft, an outside air temperature of -47 degrees Celsius, and moderate turbulence.
But moments later, after reporting precipitation started to fall and requesting to climb, they declared an emergency.
“We’re descending 8,000 – mayday, mayday - we’re descending 10,000 feet per minute,” the pilot said. “We are in an overspeed condition descending 20,000 feet per minute … We’re going to crash into the ground.”
The jet descended 27,000 feet over the course of one minute, just before flight tracking data cut off, the website ADS-B Exchange shows.
There were scattered storms in the area at the time of the crash, and the plane passed through a stronger storm cell a few minutes before it began descending. It is unclear if the storm contributed to the crash but at the time, the flight was in an area where the FAA had warned of thunderstorms and threats to aircraft, known as a convective SIGMET.
Ice on wings and other surfaces can pose a major threat to private jets. In January 2024, the NTSB published a safety alert underscoring the risks of in-flight icing conditions, which can cause pilots to lose control. The agency warned ice can “make managing the airplane’s flightpath and airspeed more difficult and can prevent the airplane from maintaining level flight.”
The road is buckled where the plane slammed into it, creating a crater, video from CNN affiliate WPBF showed.
The crash occurred near Military Trail, between Cresthaven Boulevard and 10th Avenue North, the Palm Beach County Sheriff’s Office said in a statement.
All northbound and southbound lanes of Military Trail are closed until further notice, officials said, and motorists are advised to avoid the area and seek alternate routes.
About 600 people are in need shelter because of the damage on the ground, said Joel Flores, Palm Beach County commissioner for District 3, who was the first county official at the scene. The residents are being sent to two shelters in the county while the site is being investigated, he said.
“I heard and felt the boom,” Andrew Mannino told CNN. “The power immediately went out and is still out.”
He said he smelled the smoke and “saw a large black cloud immerse in the air.”
The crash site is about four miles south of the airport in West Palm Beach, which was renamed for President Donald Trump earlier this year. It’s also about eight miles southwest of Mar-A-Lago. Trump was in West Palm Beach earlier Sunday, but departed the airport on Air Force One a little more than one hour before this crash.
Dash cam video showing the crash is going to be important to investigators piecing together what happened, said Mary Schiavo, a former inspector general for the Transportation Department.
The airport is a good place to wait out the bad weather, Schiavo told CNN’s Fredricka Whitfield Sunday. “That is not a controlled descent. That is a descent where literally you’re exceeding that the speed of the plane on descent. You’re exceeding the descent rate. So at that point, it’s clear whatever happened, they had lost control of the plane.”
The steep descent could have taken parts off the plane, and the flight recorder could have been destroyed in the explosion, Schiavo added.
It’s not clear if the plane had a cockpit voice recorder on board, which could provide key details to NTSB investigators. FAA regulations require jet aircraft with more than one engine to carry a voice recorder, but only if they are flown for hire. Records show the airplane was made available for charter flights.

Nine Killed In Florida Jet Crash As Investigators Probe Final Moments
by Stefan J. Bos, Worthy News Chief International Correspondent
PALM BEACH, USA (Worthy News) – U.S. aviation investigators were examining the final moments of a private jet Monday after all nine people aboard were killed when the aircraft plunged into a residential area in Florida, erupting into a fireball and forcing hundreds of residents from their homes.
The Learjet 60 crashed Sunday near a busy roadway in Greenacres, Palm Beach County, not far from President Donald J. Trump’s Mar-a-Lago estate, leaving a large crater and scattering burning debris across the neighborhood.
The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) said the aircraft had departed Austin-Bergstrom International Airport in Texas and was heading to North Eleuthera Airport in the Bahamas when it crashed at about 12:50 p.m. local time.
U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy confirmed that all nine people aboard had died, describing the incident as a “horrific tragedy.”
“Please join me in praying for the families and loved ones of those we lost,” Duffy wrote on social media, adding that federal aviation authorities were closely monitoring the disaster.
PILOT’S DISTRESS CALLS
Air traffic control recordings indicated that the crew reported icing, moderate turbulence and precipitation before requesting permission to climb to a higher altitude.
“We have light, clear ice that is manageable and moderate turbulence,” a pilot told air traffic controllers before conditions deteriorated.
The aircraft subsequently entered a rapid descent, with a pilot declaring an emergency as its speed increased dramatically.
“We are in an overspeed condition descending 20,000 feet per minute,” the pilot radioed before warning: “We’re going to crash into the ground.”
Flight-tracking service Flightradar24 said the jet’s descent rate exceeded 32,000 feet per minute at one point, before contact with the aircraft was lost.
GOVERNOR DESCRIBES DEVASTATION
Video footage showed the jet plunging toward the ground before exploding into a massive fireball near homes and passing vehicles.
Florida Governor Ron DeSantis described the disaster as “cataclysmic” after receiving a briefing from local authorities.
“It looked like a missile going down,” DeSantis told reporters. “It left a big crater on the side of the road.”
He said wreckage had been scattered over a considerable distance, but authorities had received no immediate reports of people on the ground being killed or injured.
Residents described a terrifying explosion, with debris striking nearby homes and flames spreading across the crash site.
HUNDREDS AFFECTED
“Debris was everywhere. Debris hit my house. Everything was on fire. The road was on fire,” resident Anthony Blackmon told local television.
The disaster also disrupted life for hundreds of residents near a mobile-home community close to the crash site.
Palm Beach County Commissioner Joel Flores said authorities were arranging emergency accommodation for about 600 people affected by the crash, with assistance from the American Red Cross.
Officials closed nearby Military Trail as emergency crews secured the wreckage and investigators prepared to examine the scene.
The National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB), which is leading the investigation with assistance from the FAA, dispatched investigators to Florida and scheduled a briefing in West Palm Beach on Monday.
AVIATION SAFETY QUESTIONS
The crash has renewed attention on the safety of private aviation in the United States, where thousands of business jets and smaller aircraft operate outside the scheduled commercial airline system.
Such flights form part of what regulators call general aviation, a broad category that includes private planes, corporate jets and recreational aircraft. General aviation has historically recorded higher fatal accident rates than scheduled airlines, although safety has improved in recent years.
According to the FAA, the general aviation fatal accident rate fell to an estimated 0.68 accidents per 100,000 flight hours in 2024, its lowest level since tracking began in 2009.
Investigators are expected to examine weather conditions, air traffic control recordings, flight data, maintenance records and the crew’s actions, particularly the reported icing and turbulence before the jet’s rapid descent.
However, officials have not established the cause of Sunday’s crash, and investigators caution against drawing conclusions before the evidence has been examined.

A Learjet crashes near Palm Beach, killing all 9 on board
sources.text:
Nine people aboard a private jet were killed when it crashed and exploded in a fireball near Palm Beach Sunday afternoon.
The plane, a Learjet built in 2004 and registered as N722BD, had departed from Austin and was on its way to the Bahamas, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said on X.
Duffy said the plane crashed in “a neighborhood near Cresthaven, FL,” which is about 10 miles from Palm Beach.
“Please join me in praying for the families and loved ones of those we lost,” he said.
The identities of those on board were not immediately available. Authorities also did not say what caused the crash. There were widespread thunderstorms in South Florida on Sunday afternoon.
Aviation weather data in the area at the time show heavy rainfall, low visibility, and moderate turbulence.
The crash occurred less than 10 miles from President Donald Trump’s Mar-A-Lago resort. The President left West Palm Beach around noon on Air Force One to attend a rally in Iowa, according to White House pool reports.
This is a developing story. Check back for updates.

sources.text:
9 Killed As Private Jet Crashes Into Florida Residential Area, 600 People Evacuated
A private jet crashed into a residential area in Florida on Sunday, 1 November. All nine people on board died after the aircraft hit the ground and caught fire.
AI-generated summary, reviewed by editors
The Learjet 60 was flying from Austin, Texas, to the Bahamas. It crashed near the Cresthaven neighbourhood in Palm Beach County at around 12:50 pm local time (17:50 GMT).
The crash site is around nine miles (14 km) from Mar-a-Lago, US President Donald Trump's resort.
Private Jet Falls From Sky And Explodes
The aircraft crashed on Military Trail, a road with several restaurants and shops. The impact left a large hole in the road. Pieces of the aircraft, broken concrete and fire were seen across the area.
A video from a vehicle's dashboard camera shows the jet falling towards the ground before a huge explosion. The video is being shared on social media, but officials have not confirmed its authenticity.
Florida Governor Ron DeSantis spoke about the crash at a news conference. He said, "When you see that video, it's a jarring thing. It's like a missile coming down, and a massive explosion, debris going everywhere."
 Slow motion video of the plane crash in Palm Beach Florida moments ago. Learjet 60 https://t.co/cwH8thiKtm
— Brian Krassenstein (@krassenstein) November 1, 2026
Nine People Die, 600 Residents Evacuated
US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy confirmed that all nine people on the plane had died. Officials have not yet shared their names.
Duffy called the crash a "horrific tragedy". He also said the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) would send a team to help the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) with the investigation.
"Please join me in praying for the families and loved ones of those we lost," Duffy added.
Palm Beach County Fire Rescue called the crash a "mass casualty incident". Local authorities also asked around 600 people living in a nearby mobile home community to leave their homes.
Road To Remain Closed For 30 Days
The crash also damaged local infrastructure, including water lines. Military Trail is expected to remain closed for at least 30 days because of the damage.
DeSantis said there were no reports of deaths or injuries among people on the ground.
Thunderstorms and heavy rain were also reported in the area around the time of the crash. However, officials have not confirmed whether the weather caused the accident.
The FAA and NTSB will investigate the crash and find out what caused the aircraft to fall.

sources.news_title: Jet crash in Florida: All nine people aboard killed, says Transportation Secretary
sources.text:
All nine people died aboard a business jet that crashed into a Florida neighborhood, U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said Sunday (November 1, 2026).
The aircraft departed from Austin, Texas, and was headed to the Bahamas. Duffy said the Federal Aviation Administration is sending a team to support the National Transportation Safety Board's investigation into the cause.
The Learjet 60 carrying nine people nose-dived into a South Florida neighborhood on Sunday (November 1, 2026) and erupted into a giant fireball that appeared to just miss homes before crashing near a busy roadway, creating a giant fiery crater in the pavement.
The aircraft had departed Austin-Bergstrom International Airport in Texas and was headed to the Bahamas, according to the Federal Aviation Administration. Authorities did not immediately say what caused the jet to go down or who was on it.
Jim Reynolds, a spokesperson for Austin-Bergstrom International Airport, said it was a private aircraft. He could not immediately provide details about who was on the flight.
“This is definitely a tragedy,” he said.
He said the tail number for the flight was N722BD.
Video shot from people inside their cars captured the terrifying moment the aircraft plunged from the sky, before striking near the roadway and exploding. Flames flickered around chunks of pavement lining the crater as people milled about, expressing shock it landed only feet from homes and only inches from passing vehicles. Thick black smoke engulfed the crash site.
It was unclear if the crash caused any damage to homes.
The crash occurred near Military Trail and 10th Avenue North. The Palm Beach County Sheriff's Office closed roads in both directions and urged motorists to avoid the area. Firefighters and other emergency personnel rushed to the scene.
A woman working nearby said electricity in the area had been out for approximately two hours following the crash.

sources.news_title: Nine Dead After $2 Million Private Jet Crashes Into Florida Neighborhood in Massive Fireball - Real News Now
sources.text:
Nine Dead After $2 Million Private Jet Crashes Into Florida Neighborhood in Massive Fireball
Nine people were killed Sunday afternoon when a private Learjet 60 plunged into a residential neighborhood in Palm Beach County, Florida, exploding into a massive fireball and scattering wreckage across a busy roadway just miles from President Trump’s Mar-a-Lago estate.
The aircraft crashed at approximately 12:50 p.m. near South Military Trail in Greenacres, leaving a large crater in the pavement and sending thick black smoke into the sky. Authorities confirmed that everyone aboard the aircraft died in the disaster.
HORRIFYING: Additional dashcam footage reportedly shows a Learjet 60 crashing at high speed and exploding in Palm Springs, Florida. https://t.co/nKjZIAzMsC
— Breaking911 (@Breaking911) November 1, 2026
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy confirmed the fatalities and described the incident as a horrific tragedy. He said federal aviation officials were monitoring the situation and assisting investigators working to determine what caused the aircraft to fall from the sky.
The Learjet 60 had departed Austin-Bergstrom International Airport in Texas and was traveling to North Eleuthera Airport in the Bahamas when the flight suddenly encountered trouble over South Florida.
The aircraft, identified by its registration number N722BD, was manufactured in 2004 and is a midsize business jet. Aircraft of the same model have been advertised on the used market for approximately $2 million, although the precise value of the destroyed jet has not been established.
Video captured by motorists showed the aircraft descending almost vertically toward the ground before striking the roadway and erupting into flames. The explosion occurred dangerously close to passing vehicles, homes and businesses.
Witnesses described hearing an enormous boom as the jet hit the pavement. The impact sent debris flying across the surrounding area and left a burning crater near utility poles and residential properties.
Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis visited the scene Sunday evening and compared the aircraft’s final descent to a missile striking the ground. He said the explosion was extraordinarily destructive and that debris had been scattered over a substantial distance.
Despite the severity of the impact, authorities reported no confirmed deaths or injuries among people on the ground as of Sunday evening.
Emergency crews quickly established a perimeter around the wreckage while firefighters worked to extinguish the flames and prevent additional hazards.
The crash occurred near the Green Acres Family Community mobile home park, prompting authorities to evacuate approximately 600 residents as investigators assessed the surrounding damage.
Officials arranged emergency assistance for displaced residents while crews examined damaged infrastructure, downed power lines and debris scattered throughout the neighborhood.
The Palm Beach County Sheriff’s Office closed Military Trail between Cresthaven Boulevard and 10th Avenue North, warning motorists that the roadway could remain inaccessible for an extended period.
Authorities said the crash created significant damage to the pavement and surrounding infrastructure, requiring extensive cleanup and repairs before normal traffic could resume.
Flight-tracking information provided by Flightradar24 revealed that the aircraft had been traveling at high altitude before entering a sudden and extremely rapid descent.
The jet departed Austin at approximately 10:37 a.m. Eastern time and proceeded toward the Bahamas. As it approached Florida’s Gulf Coast, the aircraft began descending from its cruising altitude.
At approximately 12:48 p.m., flight-tracking data showed the jet briefly climbing before entering a steep right-hand descent.
Its final recorded altitude was approximately 8,750 feet, with tracking information indicating that the aircraft was descending at a rate exceeding 32,000 feet per minute.
The dramatic loss of altitude occurred shortly before the aircraft struck the ground.
Air traffic control recordings revealed that the flight crew had reported difficult weather conditions before the crash.
The pilots informed controllers that they were experiencing icing, precipitation and turbulence, and requested a change in altitude to obtain smoother flying conditions.
Controllers authorized the requested maneuver, but the situation deteriorated rapidly.
The crew subsequently reported an excessive rate of descent and an overspeed condition as they struggled to control the aircraft.
In the final moments, a pilot warned air traffic controllers that the aircraft was going to crash.
“Holy f*ck, we’re out of time” Heart crushing ATC audio captures the moments before a Learjet 60 crashed in Palm Beach County, Florida, killing all 9 souls on board.
VIA: @thenewarea51 https://t.co/CWOtYjJqef
— Breaking911 (@Breaking911) November 1, 2026
The recording provides a disturbing account of the emergency, although investigators have not determined whether weather, mechanical problems, pilot actions or another factor caused the disaster.
Heavy rain and thunderstorms were affecting parts of South Florida at the time, with a flood watch in effect across portions of the region.
The aircraft had reportedly passed through an area of stronger storm activity shortly before the rapid descent began.
Aviation investigators will examine whether those conditions contributed to the accident, but officials have cautioned that the cause remains unknown.
The National Transportation Safety Board dispatched an investigative team to the crash site Sunday. The Federal Aviation Administration is assisting with the investigation.
Investigators are expected to examine flight data, air traffic control communications, aircraft maintenance records and physical evidence recovered from the wreckage.
They will also attempt to determine the aircraft’s condition immediately before the emergency and whether any equipment malfunction occurred during the flight.
The NTSB announced plans to hold a briefing Monday as investigators begin documenting the crash site and collecting evidence.
The identities of the nine victims had not been publicly released as of Sunday evening.
Officials have not disclosed whether the passengers were traveling for business, recreation or another purpose.
Federal records identify the aircraft’s registered owner as a Delaware-based company, but authorities have not established whether the owner was aboard the flight.
BREAKING: An aircraft crashed in Palm Beach County, Florida, scattering debris and bringing down power lines. https://t.co/2cXKM48GMS
— Breaking911 (@Breaking911) November 1, 2026
The tragedy occurred within several miles of Mar-a-Lago, President Trump’s private club and residence in Palm Beach.
According to reporting from CNN, Trump had departed the nearby airport aboard Air Force One more than an hour before the aircraft crashed. Authorities have not indicated that the president’s movements had any connection to the incident.
The crash attracted widespread attention after footage of the jet’s final descent circulated on social media.
The videos showed how narrowly the aircraft missed several vehicles traveling along the roadway, underscoring the potential for additional casualties in the densely populated area.
DeSantis praised the emergency response and emphasized the importance of assisting residents whose homes and daily routines had been disrupted.
Local authorities continued coordinating shelter arrangements, road closures and utility repairs as federal investigators prepared to examine the wreckage.
For the families of those aboard the aircraft, the disaster has left nine lives lost and many unanswered questions.
The NTSB investigation will seek to establish what caused the Learjet to lose control during what was supposed to be a routine flight from Texas to the Bahamas.
Until investigators complete their examination, the circumstances behind the aircraft’s sudden descent and catastrophic impact remain undetermined.

sources.text:
Nine dead after Learjet 60 crashes just a few miles from Donald Trump's Mar-a-Lago
The aircraft came down six miles from Donald Trump's Mar-a-Lago estate.
Nine people have died following a private aircraft disaster close to a mobile home estate, merely six miles from Donald Trump's Mar-A-Lago residence.
The Learjet 60 plummeted into a residential neighbourhood in Greenacres, Palm Beach County, at approximately 12.50pm EST (5.50pm GMT) on Sunday, officials confirmed. Reports suggest it struck a tree and severed power cables during its descent.
Officials have yet to establish what prompted the aircraft's catastrophic failure, nor have they disclosed the identities of those aboard. Jim Reynolds, a representative for Austin-Bergstrom International Airport, confirmed it was a private plane.
He was unable to immediately furnish information regarding the passengers. The Learjet 60 is a mid-sized corporate aircraft designed to carry six to seven passengers, plus two flight crew.
The jet had taken off from the Texas airport bound for North Eleuthera Airport in the Bahamas. Flight-tracking platforms lost signal after the vessel nosedived roughly 27,000ft within sixty seconds, reports the Express.
"This is definitely a tragedy," Mr Reynolds stated.

Palm Beach County authorities were evacuating about 600 people from a nearby mobile home community while federal officials investigate the crash. The road will be closed until further notice, county officials said.

Weather conditions are a "major" focus of an investigation into a weekend private plane crash that killed nine people, US transportation investigators have said.
At a briefing, Tom Chapman of the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB), retraced the ill-fated journey of the Learjet 60, which departed Austin, Texas at 3.37pm Irish time yesterday on a trip to North Eleuthera in the Bahamas.
The plane plummeted into a neighbourhood in Palm Beach County in southern Florida, killing everyone on board.
The jet was carrying a pilot, a copilot and seven passengers. Authorities have not released their identities, saying genetic analysis is needed.
US media identified the copilot as 20-year-old Nathalia Gadelha Filgeiras, who had received her pilot's license at age 17, before she received a driver's license.
Ms Filgeiras, who had already amassed 1,300 flight hours, began working for a charter plane company based in Fort Lauderdale, Florida about nine months ago.

(CNN) — Nine people died after a Bahamas-bound Learjet crashed and then erupted in a fireball in Palm Beach County, Florida, Sunday afternoon, officials said.
The crash is the second deadliest in the United States this year, according to National Transportation Safety Board records, following June’s skydiving plane crash in Butler, Missouri, which killed 12.
